title: Indonesian court bans use of education funding for free school meals
text:
Read the story in Bahasa Indonesia

Indonesia's Constitutional Court has ruled the country's flagship Free Nutritious Meals program, designed to combat under-nutrition, cannot be funded through the national education budget.

The free meals program, or MBG, was launched in 2025 with the aim of feeding 83 million school children and expectant mothers that year.

On Thursday, Indonesia's chief judge Suhartoyo ruled that the budget for educational needs and the free meals program must be separated within two years.

"Funding for the Free Nutritious Meals program, which is currently classified as a component of education spending, must be separated from operational education funding," the court said.

The ​ruling came after students and educators filed petitions against this year's state budget law, arguing that counting the free meals program as an educational provision violated Indonesia's constitution.

The court found while the provision did not breach the constitution this year, it must separate the funding allocations by no later than the 2028 state budget, but ideally earlier.

Teachers worry ruling will not be implemented

Under the constitution at least 20 per cent of Indonesia's state budget must be allocated to education.

In the 2026 budget, education spending accounted for 20.1 per cent of total expenditure.

At the centre of the case was the government's decision to allocate almost one-third of Indonesia's Rp769.1 trillion ($61.5 billion) education budget to the free meals program.

Sources of funding for the Free Nutritious Meals program. (ABC News: Jarrod Fankhauser; Indonesian Ministry of Finance)

The petitioners argued that if MBG spending were excluded, education spending would fall to about 14 per cent — well below the legal requirement.

They asked the court to ensure all of the education budget was directed to core learning functions like school facilities, teachers' salaries, classroom learning and scholarships.

The Education and Teachers' Association was one of the groups behind the challenge.

Iman Zanatul Haeri at the Constitutional Court. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

Iman Zanatul Haeri, head of teacher advocacy at the association, welcomed the court's decision but described it as "a grey area ruling".

"This kind of ruling is usually used by the government to keep a program going while making a few adjustments so it can continue operating while still complying with the constitution," Mr Haeri told ABC Indonesia.

"With this decision, the constitutional court must ensure that education funding is used for the welfare of educators, including university lecturers.

"But we also know that even in the best-case scenario there is no guarantee that the government will implement the ruling."

Mr Haeri said it was possible the government already had a plan to preserve the MBG, which it considered a priority initiative.

"We will continue to speak out until the government realises that using education funding for MBG is a fundamental constitutional mistake," he said.

Riga Felix was one of the petitioners for education funds to the Constitutional Court. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

Rega Felix, another petitioner who attended the Constitutional Court hearing, described the ruling as a "victory" for educators because it means "the education budget can no longer be interfered with by the MBG program".

He said some concerns remained.

"There are two key phrases in the ruling. Funding for MBG from the education budget is considered constitutional for 2026, but not for subsequent years," Mr Felix said.

"So I feel the Constitutional Court has still taken a middle path that remains somewhat grey. But in principle, our petition has been granted."

Mr Felix also said the court's decision to allow up to two years for the ruling to be implemented could be open to differing interpretations.

"We would prefer to see the political will start now because, in principle, this is not education spending," he said.

Some teachers paid less than $43 a month, association says

The Indonesian government plans to appoint tens of thousands of MBG's core kitchen workers as government employees. (Supplied: Nur Zaid, Kompas.com)

The test now will be whether the government fully implements the decision and redirects education funding towards schools, teachers and students.

The Institute for Demographic and Affluence (IDEAS) has previously said that the amount of money currently allocated to MBG was enough to provide free basic education for all Indonesian children, scholarships for nearly 3 million low-income university students and salary increases for more than 2 million contract teachers.

Teachers paid $170 per month as education funds go to free meals Temporary teachers in Indonesia paid low wages criticise a government decision to direct one third of yearly education funding to the president's flagship free meals program.

The Indonesian Teachers Association (PGRI), citing data from IDEAS, told parliament earlier this year that Indonesia still had at least 700,000 contract teachers.

According to the organisation, 74 per cent of those contract teachers earned less than Rp2 million ($170) a month, while some received less than Rp500,000 ($43).

"For example, in Dompu, West Nusa Tenggara, salaries are far below a decent standard, at just Rp139,000 ($11)," a PGRI representative told parliament.

Petitioners vow to see change enforced

President Prabowo Subianto inspecting the distribution of free meals in Bogor, West Java, last year. (Supplied: Presidential Secretariat Press Bureau, Cahyo)

Although the Constitutional Court has partially granted the challenge, Mr Haeri of the Education and Teachers' Association said he did not believe it would guarantee change and there was work to do.

"We will formally hand over the Constitutional Court's ruling to the state secretariat, the National Nutrition Agency, and the ministries and institutions involved in administering MBG," he told the ABC.

"We want to ensure that the executive branch truly implements the constitutional mandate, and hopefully that will lead to changes in the 2027 State Budget Law."

Petitioners celebrated the Constitutional Court's ruling prohibiting the use of education funds for MBG. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

Mr Haeri said the ruling represented an important test of the Constitutional Court's willingness to defend constitutional principles.

"We can see now whether these judges are truly guardians of the constitution or not, because a constitutional mandate is not a matter of whether it can or cannot be carried out, but a matter of obligation," he said.

" A constitutional mandate must be implemented, full stop. "

Prasetyo Hadi, Indonesia's minister of the state secretariat, said the government had received the court's ruling and would respect the decision.

"We will need to review it because budget matters are not decided by the government alone," he told reporters.

"The budget is drafted together with parliament, so please give us some time."

A group of people demonstrated in front of the Constitutional Court demanding that the government comply with the decision. (ABC News: Ari Wu)

MP Yahya Zaini, part of the ruling coalition, said the ruling should be acted on quickly, with policymakers finding a way for the MBG program to continue.

"The National Nutrition Agency must undertake major efficiency measures," Mr Zaini said.

"That includes refocusing spending, limiting the construction of new kitchens and improving the governance of the MBG program."

Meals program faces ongoing scrutiny

The National Nutrition Agency (BGN), which oversees the MBG program, has been under the spotlight in recent months.

In the lead up to the ruling there was a string of controversies involving the agency including allegations of corruption involving former BGN head Dadan Hindayana, the resignation of his successor Nanik S Deyang, and the closure of hundreds of MBG kitchens.

Indonesia's free meal program poisons thousands of children The key election commitment of President Prabowo Subianto is facing mounting backlash over its poor oversight, questionable food sourcing and unhygienic kitchens.

The government also reduced the program's budget on two occasions and said more cuts were possible.

Mr Haeri said those developments appeared less like a genuine internal review and more like an effort to adapt to the legal challenge.

"Whether this is predictive or something else, throughout the hearings we saw BGN continually trying to improve itself in line with the direction of the proceedings," he said.

"That is actually not good news, because they should have been conducting evaluations without needing to be challenged first, without us having to go to the Constitutional Court.

"The government is … revising things here and there, even though the root of the problem is that the design of BGN was flawed from the very beginning."

title: Jewish artist 'cancelled' after group chat leak, royal commission hears
text:
A Jewish Australian artist has said she was "cancelled", dropped from her residency and lost friends after the leaking of a private message in which she described terrorist group Hamas as "animals".

Representatives of Australia's arts and creative industry are fronting the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, which has been considering the use of education and training to combat hate.

The inquiry has previously heard evidence about hundreds of creatives whose information and messages were leaked in the doxxing of a private chat group in early 2024.

Nina Sanadze was involved in the collection of floral tributes following the Bondi attack. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

Melbourne artist Nina Sanadze told the inquiry a private message in which she described terrorist group Hamas as "animals" in the wake of the October 7, 2023 attack in Israel was released in the leak.

Ms Sanadze said she was immediately "dropped" from friendship groups and was told by the art institution she was attached to that it would be "inappropriate" for her to come to the studio.

She said she had told her employer before the doxxing event she would leave the studio, due to the increase in antisemitic sentiment in the community post-October 7, 2023.

"I said 'let me leave'. They were concerned it would look antisemitic … don't leave," she said.

Ms Sanadze said she was subsequently "interrogated" about her political beliefs by the art institution after the doxxing event in early 2024.

"I was told that if I did not leave the studios, there would be more … information released by unknown people, they wouldn't mention who, to discredit and damage my reputation. So I was threatened with that unless I left," she said.

Ms Sanadze went on to open the Goldstone Gallery in early 2025, saying there was "no other place for people like [her] to exhibit" their art.

The inquiry heard the gallery had hosted public events, poetry readings, live music and discussions between Palestinian and Israeli women.

The gallery is currently closed, with Ms Sanadze saying Jewish artists were hesitant to publicly exhibit their work.

"There's no funding, there's no security, it is very hard," she said.

"The artists are scared to exhibit, and it's getting worse after [the terror attack in] Bondi.

"People fear, not only for their safety but for their reputational damage."

Ms Sanadze was involved in the collection of three tonnes of floral tributes left at Bondi Pavilion after the shooting on December 14, 2025.

The vigil established at Bondi Pavilion following the December 14 terror attack.

The flowers have been transported to Melbourne, where they are being used to create an exhibition for the Sydney Jewish Museum.

Ms Sanadze said the flowers were a visible demonstration of the "outpouring and support" for the Jewish community.

"The flowers meant for me and for the Jewish community … they symbolise cohesion and empathy and standing together," she said.

Comedian told he didn't 'look Jewish'

The inquiry heard from a Jewish comedian, who used the pseudonym CGM, who shared some of the material he performs at festivals and gigs.

"Earlier this year, I was outside a bar speaking to a non-Jewish friend who said to me, 'you don't experience antisemitism do you? You don't even look Jewish'," he said.

"I asked him, 'what does Jewish look like, horns?'"

"It's true, I don't look like [Jerry] Seinfeld, but that didn't stop my synagogue in Melbourne from being … set on fire recently, or the synagogue where I did my bat mitzvah from being rammed by a car.

"Nor did it stop my workplace from being firebombed and graffitied to depict my Jewish boss with horns."

A witness described feeling "fear and shame" after the October 7, 2023 attack. (Suppied: Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion)

The comic said his peers had helped him when he started to isolate himself after October 7, 2023.

"After a few weeks, a comic with a Muslim background reached out to me and said 'where have you been?' I said I just feel like staying in … I feel so much fear and shame," he said.

"[The other comic] said to me 'brother, I've seen your act, you should have been feeling fear and shame the whole time.'

"He said 'don't be stupid, come and tell jokes.' He gave me a spot at his gig, which is a very generous thing for a comic to do."

CGM said he later told the other comic he felt "[Jewish] blood is cheap to people".

"He said [the Muslim community] feel the same," he said.

"I think there's a lot of feelings and a lot of pain. But we didn't hurt each other, we made each other laugh.

"That is one example of the best of the industry and what I hope people would want out of their arts industry.

"It is interesting to be in that nuance and that connection rather than the binary I think that's what makes great art."

title: Magpies coach throws support behind Bobby Hill as star exits
text:
Collingwood's Bobby Hill has exited the club amid support from coach Craig McRae after the premiership hero was racially abused on social media.

The Magpies have formally split with Hill, cutting short the 26-year-old's bumper contract, which was due to expire at the end of 2030.

"I'm going to take a break from football to keep working on myself and regain my passion for the game," Hill said in a statement released by the Magpies today.

Hill was the star of Collingwood's 2023 premiership under coach Craig McRae, winning the Norm Smith Medal for a four-goal grand final showing against Brisbane.

But having taken stretches of personal leave, he hasn't played at AFL level for almost a year — making just three VFL appearances in 2026.

On Thursday, before the Pies lost to Geelong at the MCG, Hill shared on Instagram a vile direct message from a Collingwood supporter that included a racist slur among other insults.

"You have disappointed this whole club and it's (sic) 100 thousand plus fans what you have done the last 18 months," the account also posted.

"… I hope nothing but the worst for you."

Hill posted a screenshot of the message and captioned it "anyone know this tough guy?"

The Magpies have publicly supported Hill throughout his turbulent period, and McRae again expressed his care for the forward's wellbeing — and disgust at those posting abusive comments on social media.

"Bobby, our thoughts are with you," McRae said after the MCG defeat on Thursday night.

"Not just for Bobby — what's going on? It's a crazy place at times, isn't it?

"I don't do social media, so bear with me, but I did look on a website which had feedback, and the feedback is unbelievable.

"It's just a cesspool for people just to vent. I find it fascinating that's actually something that people would be interested in.

"If Bobby's listening there, I'm sorry to hear that's the case. We'll always love him. It's sad to hear that."

This morning, the Pies' football manager Charlie Gardiner confirmed the end of Hill's contract.

"The club has been working with Bobby over the past 12 months to put support structures in place to help him work through some personal matters," Gardiner said in a statement.

"Despite this, Bobby has unfortunately struggled to meet his commitments to the club consistently this year and agreed that taking a break from football is the best decision for him and his family."

Meanwhile, the Magpies are counting the cost of Thursday night's loss with veteran defender Jeremy Howe suffering a fractured arm.

It is the same arm that he broke horrifically after a nasty landing from an aerial contest, also against Geelong, in 2023.

"The likelihood is he'll probably need an operation," McRae said post-game.

Utility Harry Perryman suffered a left hamstring injury — having strained his right hamstring earlier in the season.

And Brownlow medal favourite Nick Daicos has a bruised right foot, but he played out the game.

title: Are government grants enough to save Sydney's live music scene?
text:
The announced closure of a beloved inner west Sydney live music venue has prompted questions from the NSW shadow arts minister about the effectiveness of government grants trying to stem the loss of music spaces.

Erskineville dive bar MoshPit Bar announced this week it would be shutting its doors in November, citing rising operating costs and declining revenues.

The venue on Sydney's King Street nightlife strip had received more than $100,000 in NSW and federal government grants over the past few years to improve music infrastructure.

It received $64,000 from the federal government's Revive Live grant scheme last financial year to cover equipment, infrastructure and accessibility costs.

MoshPit had received government grants aimed at supporting live music. (702 ABC Sydney: Isabella Michie)

In 2024/25 it received $87,000 from NSW government to improve accessibility, ventilation, equipment and soundproofing.

It had also received $30,000 in 2023 to bill emerging bands and support rising talent from the federal government's Live Music Australia program.

MoshPit owner Mitchell McLennan said the grants made a difference in improving the venue's stage and soundproofing, but could not keep the venue open alone.

"The cost of alcohol goes up every six months and people feel it," Mr McLennan said.

"A schooner of beer's $11, it's a huge amount.

"People are just staying home."

MoshPit is on a busy nightlife strip in Sydney's inner west. (702 ABC Sydney: Isabella Michie)

Cost pressures should be addressed by grants: opposition

Shadow arts minister Chris Rath said the $87,000 NSW grant went towards "enhancing accessibility" when the venue's closure came from rising costs.

"Why weren't the actual drivers of venue considered when this grant was approved?" Mr Rath said.

"The minister needs to be able to assure the public that when a substantial amount of their taxpayer funds is invested in something, there is a transparent process for how it will deliver lasting value."

Mr Rath said the Liberal opposition would help Sydney's nightlife by cutting payroll tax for small and medium businesses.

Federal minister says grants are worth the risk

Federal Arts Minister Tony Burke told 702 ABC Sydney that investing in MoshPit through the grants was worth the risk.

"Even though they're private venues, every extra bit of assistance at the moment makes a difference," Mr Burke said.

"It is devastating when we lose one, but we are determined to make sure that that live culture throughout the country is something that survives.

"You've just got to take the risk and keep investing and keep providing because for a whole lot of venues, that investment actually will be the difference."

Mr Burke announced on Thursday another $12 million was being put into the Revive Live grant scheme to back venues across the country.

NSW Arts Minister John Graham was approached for comment.

The NSW Labor government gave $5.1 million to 39 venues in 2024/25 to upgrade music venues' soundproofing, energy efficiency and AV equipment.

Concerns over number of live music venues

Joe Hardy, who co-founded Sydney's most comprehensive gig guide SydneyMusic.net, said of the 373 different venues that put on gigs last financial year, just 19 hosted 100 or more shows, including MoshPit Bar.

Mr Hardy said it was disturbing that Sydney was losing venues that consistently put on live music.

"That is where I start getting into red flashing alarm bells territory," Mr Hardy said.

"Venues in their successful eras gone by were always uniquely the hosts of communities, they weren't just spaces for hire."

Mr Hardy said he was seeing live music take off in non-traditional spaces where the government live music grant programs may have been overlooking.

"I think punter preferences are changing," Mr Hardy said.

"I don't think that throwing stimulus money at venues is necessarily going to save the venues.

"We kind of need to think bigger in terms of what people are actually looking for and I think especially from the perspective of punter preferences."

title: How a classification change ended Korey's Commonwealth Games hopes
text:
As the track cycling competition at the 2026 Commonwealth Games gets underway, Australians expecting to see Paralympic champion Korey Boddington in action will be left disappointed.

The popular para cyclist, who won the kilometre C4-5 time trial in Paris, has joined swimmer Alexa Leary as another high-profile para athlete removed from the Glasgow Games after a reclassification of his disability.

Leary, the reigning S9 100m world record holder, was to make her Commonwealth Games debut in Scotland but was reclassified as an S10 athlete earlier this year.

Partly due to the stripped-down nature of these Games, there are no sprint freestyle events for S10 swimmers at the Tollcross pool, with the only event in that category being the 200-metre individual medley, which Leary does not compete in.

Boddington, the reigning Sir Hubert Opperman Trophy winner and 2025 Australian cyclist of the year, was also reclassified, twice in the space of a year, first becoming eligible to compete, and then ineligible.

Boddington's year as a C3 athlete

Korey Boddington is the world record holder in the kilo at C3 and C4 classifications. (Supplied: Cycling New Zealand)

Classification for para athletes has long been a contentious and complicated issue.

The process exists in para sport to enable athletes with different impairment types — not necessarily the same disabilities — the chance to compete on a relatively level playing field.

"International classification is conducted by a panel comprising medical classifiers and technical classifiers before a competition, after which they will be informed which class they are in and why," AusCycling told ABC Sport in a statement.

"Their role is to assess whether an athlete has an eligible impairment that meets the minimum impairment criteria for Para cycling, assess the extent to which the athlete is able to execute the specific tasks and activities fundamental to Para cycling, and, where required, undertake observation in competition assessment."

Within the classification framework imposed by the sport's governing body, the UCI, Boddington — who won two Paralympic medals as a C4 athlete — was, briefly, reclassified as a C3 athlete in 2025.

This indicates a higher level of impairment than under which he competed in Paris. In cycling, the scale is from 1-5, where 1 is the most severe impairment and 5 the least.

This is not uncommon.

Boddington only made his first national team appearance in the Paralympic year of 2024.

He endeared himself to the Australian public with his love of burritos, enjoying up to four of them a day: "You know how many carbs are in the wrap, and you can specifically portion out all your protein that are on them," he told AusCycling in 2025 by way of explanation.

It earned him the affectionate nickname the Flying Burrito.

Korey Boddington was a breakout star of the Paris Paralympics. (Getty Images: PA Images/Andrew Matthews)

For an athlete like Boddington, who lives with an acquired brain injury and had not spent all that long in the sport, it is understandable that his classification level was still being sorted out.

But having been reclassified, Boddington promptly won four world championship gold medals as a C3 athlete at the 2025 world championships in Rio, winning the men's sprint, 1,000-metre (kilo) time trial and elimination race before helping Australia clinch victory in the mixed C1-5 team sprint.

The 30-year-old Queenslander, the world record holder for the C4 flying 200m sprint time trial, also broke world records in the C3 flying 200m sprint and the C3 kilo at the Oceania Championships in Cambridge, New Zealand in February this year.

He won four gold medals in total at those championships: the kilo, sprint, individual pursuit and mixed C1-5 team sprint, as well as winning silver medals in the elimination and scratch races.

All signs were pointing towards Boddington competing in the C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events at the Games in Glasgow.

However, upon his return from New Zealand, Boddington was reclassified a C4 athlete and competed in that category at the TrackNats in Brisbane in late March.

Boddington still won gold in the sprint, elimination, scratch, kilo and C1-C5 team sprint at the Anna Meares Velodrome.

However, there are only four men's para cycling events set to be contested on the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow; none of which C4 athletes are eligible for — the sprint and 1,000m time trial in the tandem B category, and the 3,000m individual pursuit and 1,000m time trial events in the C1-3 classification.

Classification can be 'tough'

Korey Boddington won gold in the men's C4 1,000m time trial at the 2024 Paralympic Games in Paris. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Being rubbed out of a major competition like the Commonwealth Games, the only multi-sport event where able-bodied and para athletes compete on the same program, through no fault of their own, is a bitter pill for the athletes to swallow.

And classification can be a very sensitive and personal process.

A Four Corners investigation in 2023 found that some Paralympic athletes were deliberately exaggerating their impairments in a bid to win medals and that the system itself was ripe for manipulation.

Australians embroiled in Paralympics scandal Former athletes and officials tell Four Corners the system of Paralympic classification is flawed and easily manipulated.

AusCycling said it took care to ensure that its athletes are educated about classification throughout their time in the sport.

That takes the form of education about the classification system itself, guidance from classification experts, discussion of possible classification outcomes, and planning for different scenarios.

"The focus is on ensuring athletes understand the UCI Classification Rules, including eligible impairments, sport class profiles and assessment methods, while continuing to focus on their development and performance goals," the statement read.

The statement also noted that "not all classification outcomes can be anticipated, particularly for more complex impairment profiles".

Classification for para athletes can take place over the course of an athlete's career to ensure they are in their correct category for competition.

They may also have to be tested if the criteria for their classification change or if the governing body changes its tests. In cycling, that falls under the UCI's jurisdiction.

When a classification panel allocates a sport class to an athlete, it also assigns a status to that status: confirmed, review at the next available opportunity, review with a fixed review date or expired.

Needless to say, most athletes have to go through the process multiple times during their career.

Double world champion Tara Neyland detailed the process of classification. (Supplied: AusCycling)

Two-time world champion on the road and three-time track world champion Tara Neyland, who is also competing in the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome at these Games, said in a detailed Instagram video in May that classification days can be incredibly tough.

Neyland lives with facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness, which means her level of impairment is likely to change over time.

"Being a progressive degenerative condition, they need to keep reassessing as my body will keep changing," Neyland said in her Instagram video.

AusCycling noted that in instances such as Neyland's, athletes can request a medical review, but it is not imposed by AusCycling out of competition if it is against the athlete's wishes.

Regardless, the process is clearly incredibly emotionally draining for the athletes involved.

"Classification day is a tough one," Neyland said.

"Essentially you're being assessed, being graded, for your level of impairment of your condition, disability, injury, whatever it may be, however you define it.

"It can bring up a lot of emotions.

"It's a necessary part of para sport so that we can be as fairly graded as possible, but it's still quite challenging.

"For me, until coming into para sport, I've tried to view myself as someone who's incredibly capable, and then to flip the mindset and have to prove your level of impairment and speak to all your challenges and struggles and areas that, for me, weaken, struggle to do the same things that an able body can do is hard."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

AusCycling said it was committed to helping athletes with any issues that arose from classification changes.

"Ultimately, classification exists to protect the integrity and fairness of Para sport," AusCycling's statement read.

"While the prospect of reclassification can be challenging, particularly given its potential impact on competitive opportunities and performance goals, AusCycling remains committed to prioritising athlete wellbeing and supporting athletes' continued performance throughout the entire process.

"Athlete wellbeing remains a key priority throughout any classification review process, whether anticipated or unexpected.

"Appropriate support is identified both on the ground and remotely to ensure athletes are well supported throughout the process."

title: 'It was weird': De Minaur beats Hewitt in Aussie tussle
text:
Alex de Minaur has cast aside sentiment to end Cruz Hewitt's breakout run and storm into the Washington Open quarter-finals.

The top seed and defending champion produced a clinical display to defeat the 17-year-old Hewitt, son of former world number one Lleyton, 6-2, 6-3 in just 61 minutes.

De Minaur shared a warm embrace with Hewitt at the net as Lleyton looked on from the stands at Stadium Court.

"It was definitely weird," de Minaur said.

"I knew I was going to play him on the tour some day, but I didn't actually expect it to be this week. It was an amazing feeling."

Cruz Hewitt has breakthrough Tour win Cruz Hewitt wins for the first time at ATP Tour level, his Washington upset of former world number 37 Marcus Giron set to rocket him up the tennis rankings.

A Wimbledon boys' finalist this month, Hewitt idolised de Minaur while growing up around the Davis Cup team captained by his father.

"Even [with] all the lead-up, seeing all the incredible pictures that we have together and how we've grown up, I'm glad I managed to get through," de Minaur said.

"But I'm sure we're going to have many battles in the years to come."

Australia's world number six charged to the net with authority and displayed great hands en route to improving his win-loss record to 29-14 this season.

Despite his defeat, Hewitt is set to soar some 252 spots in the rankings to a fresh career high of about world number 360 after qualifying in Washington and then winning his maiden ATP match.

Competing for the first time since marrying British WTA star Katie Boulter this month, de Minaur next faces American Brandon Nakashima, who ousted seventh-seed Jakub Mensik 7-6 (5), 3-6, 6-4 to reach his second consecutive Washington quarter-final.

Nakashima holds a 2-1 edge over the Australian, with de Minaur's lone win against the American also coming in last year's quarter-finals before he went on to lift the title.

title: Nearly 350km of NT highway still closed months after flood damage
text:
Nearly 350 kilometres of a Northern Territory highway remains closed due to flood damage, several months after it was damaged in the wet season, with no repairs undertaken.

The Sandover Highway is closed from Ammaroo cattle station, about 300km north-east of Alice Springs, all the way to the Queensland border.

Owner Stewart Weir claimed repair work had not started and said the closure had significantly impacted his business, with cattle trucks forced to take vast detours.

"It hasn't been touched at all this year, and it's basically impassable," he said.

" That road has not even had an opening grade, or anything on it, which personally I don't think is good enough. "

Stewart Weir owns Ammaroo Station and other properties in the region. (ABC Rural: Jack Price)

Mr Weir said the road, most of which is unsealed, was an important route for multiple cattle stations and the residents of remote Aboriginal communities.

"It's not good for the region. The locals travel a lot between Ammaroo, (the community of) Utopia, Lake Nash Station etc," he said.

"It's hard work for them as well, on a washed-out road."

The Department of Logistics and Infrastructure was contacted multiple times for comment, and has yet to provide a response.

The Sandover Highway is used by many pastoralists to transport cattle to Queensland. (Supplied: Road Report NT)

$100m plan delayed

The NT endured a significant 2025/26 wet season, with multiple floods and cyclones, and several major roads were damaged.

The NT government launched a $100 million flood recovery fund, sourced from its budget, but only $12.5 million has been allocated to projects.

This includes flood mitigation infrastructure in the towns of Katherine and Alice Springs, as well as $500,000 towards developing a plan to relocate Daly River.

A $30.5 million road repair package was also announced, and it is understood this funding has been fully spent.

Elkedra Station was heavily impacted by flooding, and the local road was only recently repaired. (Supplied: Amber Driver)

NT Cattlemen's Association chief executive Romy Carey said the industry was frustrated by the uncertainty in the final months of the dry season.

"We'd like to see that money allocated and that planning work done," she said.

"Roads have been a key issue for the cattle industry … this is not a new topic for us and for our members.

" We need to see that money out on the roads now, time is ticking, the wet season will be here before we know it. "

The NT minister responsible for the flood recovery fund, Jo Hersey, said she was negotiating with federal minister and NT senator Malarndirri McCarthy on potential funding partnerships.

A federal government spokesperson said the flood recovery fund was a matter for the territory government.

The spokesperson said further negotiation was unnecessary and extra money could be accessed through the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements (DRFA).

The Commonwealth, the states and territories jointly fund DRFA.

"The Northern Territory government's flood recovery fund was announced without engagement with or the involvement of the Australian government," the spokesperson said.

"If the Northern Territory requires further support. They do not need to negotiate; they need to make a DRFA application."

title: Anthropic's Claude AI model hacks three companies during safety tests
text:
Artificial intelligence firm Anthropic says its Claude AI model hacked the systems of three external organisations during testing, ​days after ‌rival company OpenAI revealed a rogue agent had gone on a days-long ‌hacking spree at ⁠AI firm Hugging Face.

Claude gained ‌unauthorised ​access to ‌the other companies' systems during cybersecurity evaluations after a misconfiguration allowed the models to reach the ​internet ‌from testing environments that were supposed to be ⁠isolated, Anthropic ‌said in a statement.

The AI firm did not name the three companies involved but said it had been in contact with two of them and was working with them to patch their systems, while continuing to reach out to the third.

Loading...

The incidents were identified after ‌Anthropic reviewed its logs from more than 140,000 cybersecurity evaluation tests, a process ‌it ​launched following ⁠OpenAI's disclosures.

The tests in question involved tasking Claude with a "capture-the-flag" challenge, a method for assessing the cybersecurity capabilities of AI models.

In a capture-the-flag challenge, the model is primed with a fictional scenario and told it must recover a piece of secret information (the "flag") from a different machine.

"In all cases, Anthropic's evaluation prompt specified to Claude that its environment was a simulation and that it had no internet access," Anthropic said in its statement. "Due to a misunderstanding between us and our evaluation partner, this was not the case, and internet access was available. "Because of this, when Claude’s search led it to real systems on the open internet, it treated them as part of the exercise."

The fact that Claude was mistakenly provided with internet access, rather than configuring its own access, means the incident is likely to be considered less serious than last week's breach at OpenAI, in which a model exploited a zero-day vulnerability to escape its own testing environment.

The company also said that in one of the three hacking instances, involving an internal research test model, the model realised it was accessing real online systems that were not part of the simulated scenario, and ceased its attack.

The incident will nevertheless intensify calls for stronger controls in both internal and third-party testing environments, as AI models become increasingly capable of acting as autonomous agents in the online world.

CEO Dario Amodei (left) founded Anthropic after clashing with OpenAI's Sam Altman over AI safety. (Supplied: Futures Forum)

Anthropic has worked to differentiate itself from other AI companies by emphasising its intention to make Claude a "genuinely good, wise and virtuous" AI agent, and by restricting the rollout of its cybersecurity-focused Mythos model to a limited number of organisations, including the Australian government.

It recently clashed with the US government over the potential use of its technology to power autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, leading US President Donald Trump to issue a directive to federal agencies to cease all use of the firm's technology.

However, the company has also been criticised for changes to its data retention policies, as well as its public campaign against so-called "open models", which critics say appears designed to limit competition and pressure governments to introduce regulations that work in its favour.

The ABC recently informed staff it would allow its journalists to access Anthropic's general Claude model to assist with research and administration from September, while reiterating that AI would not be used to draft or write articles or scripts.

title: England hires NZ's Fleming to coach men's Test side, Root as captain
text:
English cricket has turned to another New Zealander to coach the men's Test team, hiring former Kiwi star Stephen Fleming, while batting great Joe Root has been reappointed as captain.

Fleming replaced his former teammate Brendon McCullum, who was fired after losing the Ashes series in Australia 4-1 over the winter and, last month, losing at home to New Zealand 2-1.

England now has an all-New Zealand coaching set-up, with McCullum remaining in charge of the one-day and Twenty20 teams.

Fleming will not take charge until after Pakistan's three-Test tour, which begins on August 19 in Leeds. McCullum's former assistant, Marcus Trescothick, will be the interim England coach for that series.

Root was previously the permanent Test captain from 2017-22 in a national record 65 Tests. He won a record 27 of those matches but has won only one of his past 18 in charge.

The 35-year-old Root formally replaces Ben Stokes, who retired suddenly from international cricket after the New Zealand series in June. Stokes had endorsed his vice-captain, Harry Brook, as the next captain.

McCullum sacked as Test coach The architect of England's controversial Bazball approach to Test cricket is given his marching orders after a disappointing string of results.

Fleming said he was excited to work with Root and Brook, adding: "I know what it feels like to have the weight of leadership and international cricket take their toll."

Fleming was New Zealand's longest-serving captain across 80 Tests and he won 28 of them. He played for three English county teams and won a league title with Nottinghamshire in 2005.

"English cricket gave that to me and it is a privilege to have this chance to give something back," he said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The England and Wales Cricket Board said it was allowing Fleming to spend time with family as he stepped down from his role at the Chennai Super Kings only this month.

Fleming led Chennai to a record five titles and 10 finals in the Indian Premier League. He also coached sister franchises in South Africa and the United States.

He will prepare England for three Tests in South Africa in December-January.

Fleming has only seven Tests in charge to ready England for the home Ashes series next year.

title: Quick hits: Tongan dance moves bring joy, David Beckham hits the velodrome
text:
A para athletics race will be run again amid much drama, a Tongan weightlifter thrills the crowd with his dancing, and Nigeria wins the fashion stakes at the velodrome.

Here are the quick hits from day seven of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Para athletics race to be re-run

Eliza Ault-Connell was knocked out of the women's 1500m T54 final. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

After a dramatic crash that took out two athletes, a disqualification that reordered the medal spots, and a subsequent protest, para athletics officials ordered a re-race of the women's 1,500m T54 final.

The race was thrown into chaos early on when Australian Eliza Ault-Connell went down heavily in a nasty crash, with Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse also knocked out of contention.

Canadian Nandini Sharma, who went on to finish second across the line, was disqualified for causing the crash.

After having that medal taken off her, Australia's Mikaela Dingley was promoted into the bronze medal position.

However, Australia and Mauritius protested the decision and, after Athletics Canada's appeal was dismissed, authorities decided to re-run the race, with some commentators saying it should have been stopped at the time of the crash.

Sharma will not be able to take to the start, with Canada saying it was "disappointed" in the decision.

"Having considered the multiple appeals that were submitted, the Jury has decided that the disqualification will stand," the statement read.

"While Athletics Canada is disappointed with this decision, we accept the process and look forward to Nandini competing again in the T53/54 400m race."

The re-race will be held on Friday 7:24pm AEST.

2. World record falls

Tara Neyland broke her own C4 4,000m Individual Pursuit world record. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australian para cyclist Tara Neyland laid down a stunning time to top qualifying in the women's C4-C5 4,000m individual pursuit qualifying, setting a world record.

Her factored time was 4:45.796, achieved at an average speed of 49.716km/h.

Neyland later returned to the track to win gold in the final.

The 32-year-old is already a three-time world champion on the track and a two-time world champion on the road.

The women's individual pursuit distance officially moved from 3,000m to 4,000m on January 1, 2025, so competing at this distance is still relatively new.

Which perhaps accounts for England's Morgan Newbury breaking the world record in the C5 classification qualification period.

3. Tonga's dancing weightlifter

Josh Uikilifi treated spectators to his best dance moves. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

If weightlifting medals were handed out for post-lift moves, Tonga's Joshua Uikilifi would have topped the podium.

Uikilifi had the SEC Armadillo crowd eating out of the palm of his hand as he competed in the men's 110kg classification.

He treated spectators to some spectacular dance moves after each successful lift.

Uikilifi produced a total of 331kg to finish fourth behind Fiji's Taniela Rainibogi, who won gold with a Games record of 378kg.

4. Nigerian para cyclists turn heads

The Nigerians were the best dressed at the velodrome on day seven. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Australia dominated the medals on the opening day at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome, but it was Nigeria which turned heads.

The Nigerian para cyclists hit the track in eye-catching uniforms, reportedly inspired by the kit worn by the national men's football team at the 2018 FIFA World Cup.

Oyindamola Abdullahi Tijani and pilot Okeyah Bethel looked magnificent as they contested the men's tandem B 1,000m time trial.

They deservedly got the seal of approval across social media platforms.

For the record, Tijani and Bethel finished fifth in the final.

Scotland's Neil Fachie (pilot: Aaron Pope) won gold ahead of James Ball (Matthew Rotherham) of Wales.

Australia's Kane Perris (Luke Zaccaria) took bronze.

5. Ronaldo and Beckham in the velodrome

If you thought the only sightings of David Beckham and Ronaldo at a major global sporting event were going to be in North America this year, then we have news for you.

Yes, that's right, David Beckham and Ronaldo were at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow, a stone's throw away from the footballing theatre of Celtic Park.

Well, David Beckham Elkatohchoongo and Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam were there, joining Rojit Singh Yanglem in India's team sprint squad.

"My father was a footballer in the national team, and he was a huge fan of David Beckham," Elkatohchoongo told AFP in 2023 at the Asian Games.

"When I was born in the hospital, they told my mum: if it's a boy, then it's David Beckham."

Laitonjam was also named after a footballer, not actually Ronaldo but Ronaldinho.

His father had, according to AFP, made a bet with his work colleagues that the Brazilian would score against England in the 2002 World Cup match they were watching.

The Barcelona legend promptly did, and minutes later Laitonjam senior received a phone call telling him that his wife was in labour.

"Just as the ball went in the goal, I must have started making an appearance," Laitonjam told The Hindu newspaper.

"I think my dad won some money that day. That's probably why I got that name. He felt I was very lucky for him."

David and Ronaldo could not add the necessary star power to the Indian team their namesakes may have demanded, though, finishing seventh and last in qualifying.

title: Mayor's failed defamation lawsuit a 'glimpse into the future', academic says
text:
A public policy academic says social media is the "new town hall" and has called for clearer "rules of engagement" after a Tasmanian mayor's failed defamation lawsuit.

Launceston Mayor Matthew Garwood took to Facebook this week saying he "respectfully" disagreed with a magistrate's decision, after a court ruled in favour of the defendant.

Court documents show on July 28 last year, Trevallyn local Ray Norman circulated a photo of a car in a disability parking spot that he had digitally altered to include Cr Garwood's photo, contact information and wrongful claim he had misused a disability parking space in Launceston.

The captions included: "Bung on the bling and expect to be treated like a bloody celebrity."

The photo of the car was originally posted on a Facebook page by another person under the comment "the lord mayor of the mall", but Mr Norman "assumed" the post was referring to Cr Garwood, deputy chief magistrate Ken Stanton said in his ruling.

Mr Norman modified the photo "without doing any research as to the owner of the car shown in that post", Magistrate Stanton said.

The modified photo was then emailed to Launceston councillors and Tasmanian MLC Rosemary Armitage.

Matthew Garwood was not present for Wednesday's court hearing at the Launceston Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Michael Brooks)

"The evidence establishes and the parties agree that the original Facebook post was not referring to the claimant [Cr Garwood] at all. The claimant had no connection to the car shown in that post," Magistrate Stanton said in his judgment.

Councillor Garwood, who self-represented in court, was seeking $15,000 for reputational damage, emotional distress and diversion of resources.

However, deputy chief magistrate Ken Stanton ruled in favour of Mr Norman.

"If any [reputational] harm was caused or likely, I consider it would be, at most, minor harm," he wrote.

"While it might be accepted that the email was inappropriate, unreasonable, prejudiced and malicious in its tone and content, that is not sufficient to establish the claim in defamation."

'This one beat me'

In a post on his Facebook page after the decision was handed down, Cr Garwood said the matter had taken a toll.

"If I had my time again, I probably wouldn't go through this process," he said.

"This one beat me. I have no problem owning that."

The mayor was not present for Wednesday's court hearing due to a local citizenship ceremony.

Cr Garwood said he was concerned that his experience would deter others from running for public office.

"Holding public office should never mean accepting elevated and targeted personal attacks," he said.

" Respectfully, I am genuinely baffled by the outcome. "

'New rules of engagement'

Without commenting specifically on the Garwood v Norman case, University of Tasmania Professor of Management David Adams said cases like it provided a "glimpse into the future".

"We're likely to see more of this happening. We're likely to see it happening more quickly. We're likely to see the increased use of AI to enhance arguments that are being presented," he said.

" We need to think how to simultaneously better protect our elected members from unnecessary criticism and at the same time better enable our citizens to engage in that civil discourse. "

Professor Adams believed the vast majority of social media users were unaware of defamation laws.

"Historically … these sort of debates would have played out in a town hall and some of the language in there probably would have been defamatory," he said.

"But social media is the new town hall, and we now need to sort out what these new rules of engagement are."

title: Burst water main causes power outages and disruptions in Adelaide CBD
text:
A burst water main that flooded an electrical substation has caused power and water outages across the Adelaide CBD, affecting businesses, a hospital and a school.

SA Water crews have been on Grenfell Street to repair a water main break since 2am on Friday.

SA Power Networks (SAPN) said the burst main flooded a substation in Coromandel Place.

"We have a substation in Coromandel Place, which is essentially across from Rundle Place Shopping Centre, and the water from that burst main has essentially flooded part of the Coromandel Place substation and that has, of course, triggered safety equipment," SAPN's Cecilia Schutz told 891 ABC Adelaide.

SA Water says repair works in Adelaide's CBD are expected to continue throughout the day. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

An SAPN spokesperson said safety mechanisms activated within the substation to shut it down, causing an outage for approximately 1,200 city customers.

The spokesperson said the Calvary Hospital was affected but "as a matter of priority" electricity was restored by 8:12am.

They said crews were able to "reroute" other power supplies to restore electricity to 600 customers but as at 8:15am, more than 500 remained without power.

Cecilia Schutz says it is an unusual occurrence. (ABC News: Sophie Landau)

"We do hope to make progress throughout the day but … it will take some days before this substation is operational again," Ms Schutz said.

"This is the first time that I have seen in many years a flooding incident in a substation in the CBD — this is an unusual circumstance, yet we are prepared for it through contingency, but electricity and water never mix and the safety of our crews and the community is of paramount importance."

As at 7:30am, traffic restrictions were in place on Grenfell Street, with the northbound left bus lane closed between Gawler Place and Twin Street.

Businesses like shops in Rundle Place are without power. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

The SA Department for Education closed Adelaide Botanic High School for the day, as the school, with about 1,200 students, was also left without power.

"Following an assessment of the situation and in order to ensure student and staff safety, a decision has been made to close the school for the day," an education department spokesperson said.

"Parents are being advised of the situation by the school."

A Calvary Hospital spokesperson said it had a generator that provided electricity but some elective surgeries were cancelled and had to be rescheduled.

'Some time' before power, water restored

SA Water general manager David Coombe said it was supporting Rundle Place shopping mall, which is currently without water.

"There's some high voltage power that we're dealing with here on Grenfell Street and a lot of other services underground which slows our ability to be able to repair it quickly," he said.

"We have a vacuum truck here at Grenfell Street and certainly at the substation extracting the water. Unfortunately, we've had inundation into one property within the Rundle [Place] plaza."

Mr Coombe said it was "quite a complex repair".

"We're working as quickly as we can but we expect it could be into the early hours of the evening before we'll be able to finalise repairs," he said.

He said early indications were that it appeared that there had been a split in the pipe.

"Quite often at this time of year with changing soil conditions, movement of soil, we can see that water mains do break — the pipe moves and soil moves away from the water main, we lose a bit of support there, but it looks as though the pipe has split," Mr Coombe said.

Work is underway to restore power and water across the CBD. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

An SA Water spokesperson said they were helping SAPN to assess the damage and required repairs, while their crews were also on site "supporting impacted customers and property owners".

"The incident was reported during the early hours of this morning, with a field technician arriving on site at approximately 2am to begin turning the water off," an SA Water spokesperson said.

"The break has resulted in water entering several nearby properties and facilities, including some basements or underground areas."

An SAPN spokesperson said flooding to the substation meant it would "not be safe for SA Power Networks to restore power to the substation for some time".

"We continue to work on finding alternate supply for customers who remain affected by the outage but we are urging city workers whose offices are affected to work from home if that is possible," the spokesperson said.

"We will be moving mobile generation into the areas of most critical need. We aim to restore supply to all customers by the end of today and we will continue to provide updates as this work progresses."

title: Australian rock music journalist Glenn A Baker dies
text:
Australian music journalist, historian and broadcaster Glenn A Baker has died aged 74.

Known for his vast music knowledge, Baker won the BBC's Rock Brain of the Universe three times in the mid-1980s.

In the mid-1970s, Baker was part of a research project which resulted in the formation of 2JJ, which later became triple j.

His radio career began hosting a trivia program on the station before moving on to Triple M.

The Archibald Prize entry of Glenn A Baker in black and white by Nafisa won the Packing Prize in 2010. (Art Gallery of NSW)

He was the manager of the band Ol'55 and in 1979, co-established Australian record label Raven Records.

Baker was also the editor of Billboard magazine for more than 20 years, wrote 17 books, as well as sleeve notes for more than 600 albums.

Known for his collection of distinctive brimless hats, he said he owned 80,000 records and about 30,000 CDs.

A portrait of Baker by artist Nafisa won the 2010 Archibald Packing Room Prize.

Music 'brought him joy'

His son, Orson told 702 ABC Sydney his father had experienced a "period of illness" and was "declining for a while".

Orson said his father had previously experienced a stroke.

He described Baker as "somebody who absolutely grabbed life, throttled it, and did everything that he wanted to do".

His son said Baker lived a "somewhat nomadic life as a child", travelling frequently across regional New South Wales.

"Subsequently I think music became something he could cling to, something that brought him joy," he said.

Baker was a prominent music industry commentator.

According to his biography, Baker left school aged 15 to "help support his family" and he was "galvanised" by seeing the Beatles on TV.

"Growing up, the most exciting thing was going out to purchase a new record to bring that record home, to open it up and to read the inner sleeve, the comments, the notes by the band, the photos," Orson said.

" And then to sit there and play it ... play the entire album start to finish, this was his world. "

"He visited over 150 countries, became an accomplished travel writer, and I guess music was his absolute passion," he said, noting Australian music was a particular focus of interest.

Orson Baker says music brought his dad joy. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

His death was announced this morning on social media by fellow music journalist Stuart Coupe.

"I'm beyond sad," Coupe posted.

"This is a post that I was hoping I wouldn't be making."

A post on his Facebook profile said he died three days after his birthday.

Created a home filled with 'music and chaos'

Baker had six children and 13 grandchildren.

Orson described their family home as being filled with "music and chaos".

"He was an avid record collector, a collector of all things music, so it was hectic.

"The strongest memory I think all of us children will have of him, was when we were all young, he took it upon himself to take each child overseas and enjoy an experience into his world.

"He was always very keen to bring his children along as a plus one to concerts and he'd drag you backstage to say, meet Mariah Carey, or whoever it may be."

Amplia Therapeutics has received encouraging lab results which highlighted the use of its lead drug narmafotinib, saying it can attack several of the nastier features that make the cancer so hard to treat. The research, led by Professor Paul Timpson and colleagues at Sydney’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research, was the results of extensive laboratory work on narmafotinib in pancreatic cancer models and was posted online on the biology preprint server bioRxiv. Amplia Therapeutics’ says fresh preclinical research data has strengthened the case for its drug candidate narmafotinib against pancreatic cancer cells, pictured. Amplia says the work adds further evidence that narmafotinib, a focal adhesion kinase (FAK) inhibitor, may improve outcomes by targeting tumour fibrosis, chemotherapy resistance and metastatic spread - three big hurdles in a disease that remains one of cancer medicine’s toughest assignments. FAK is a protein inside cells that acts like a control switch for movement, survival and attachment. It sits where cells anchor to their surrounding environment and helps tell them whether to grow, move or shut themselves down.

Advertisement

‘The research conducted by Professor Timpson’s team over recent years is now being shared with the broader scientific community.’ Amplia Therapeutics chief executive office and managing director Dr Chris Burns In many cancers, FAK becomes overactive or over-produced, helping tumour cells survive, move and spread. That has made it a target for cancer-fighting drugs such as narmafotinib. Among the key findings, the paper reported reduced tumour fibrosis and enhanced anti-tumour activity when narmafotinib was combined with chemotherapy. Other results included reduced cancer dissemination and metastatic spread in a pancreatic cancer model and the down-regulation – or diminished activity - of multiple genes linked to chemotherapy resistance. In this case, the drug appears to turn down genes that usually help cancer cells resist chemotherapy. The effect is to weaken the cancer cells’ defences, leaving chemotherapy better able to do its job and potentially lowering the number of cancer cells that remain alive after treatment. Amplia Therapeutics chief executive officer and managing director Dr Chris Burns said: “These studies strengthen the scientific rationale for the clinical development of narmafotinib and provide further insight into the multifaceted mechanisms through which narmafotinib can act in the treatment of this devastating disease.”

Advertisement

The update follows a busy clinical run for the Melbourne-based biotech. In May, Amplia launched the first stage of a Phase 2b registration-enabling pancreatic cancer study that will test daily dosing of narmafotinib with the chemotherapy drugs gemcitabine and Abraxane in newly diagnosed advanced pancreatic cancer patients. A registration-enabling study is a pivotal clinical trial designed to produce the core evidence needed to support an application for approval to market a new drug. Its job is to show that a treatment is safe at the proposed dose, that it helps patients and that the data package is strong enough for regulators such as the US Food and Drug Administration or Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration to assess. The study is expected to enrol 12 patients across two dose cohorts at three or four Australian sites, with patient enrolment planned for the fourth quarter of this year. Amplia’s June quarterly also underlined why the company is pressing ahead. Mature ACCENT trial data presented at the American Association for Cancer Research showed favourable safety and encouraging efficacy for narmafotinib, with a 36 per cent overall response rate and a 70 per cent disease control rate, compared with 50 per cent for chemotherapy alone. The data also showed median overall survival of 11.1 months — an improvement of more than two months — and progression-free survival of 7.7 months when narmafotinib was used with standard chemotherapy.

Advertisement

The company ended the June quarter with $24 million in cash, giving it a handy buffer as it pushes narmafotinib further into pancreatic cancer and prepares to test the same drug in a second oncology target. That expansion comes through PRROSE, a phase two trial being run under an agreement with the Australia New Zealand Gynaecological Oncology Group (ANZGOG) to evaluate narmafotinib alongside standard chemotherapy in 15 to 20 patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer. For Amplia, the latest paper is not a clinical result — but it is another useful building block. And in a field where every extra piece of biological support counts, the company will no doubt be happy to bank more evidence as it heads toward the next stage of its pancreatic cancer program. title: Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing
text:
Advertisement

Updated TechnologyAI Anthropic’s Claude AI hacked three real companies during testing David Swan Updated July 31, 2026 — 1:08pm ,first published July 31, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic has revealed its Claude artificial intelligence models broke into the computer systems of three real companies during safety testing, days after rival OpenAI disclosed a similar failure. The models were told they were working inside a sealed practice environment with no connection to the internet, but a set-up error meant they were not. When Claude went hunting for a way into its practice target and found real companies instead, it treated them as part of the game and broke in. On June 13, Anthropic suspended worldwide access to its two most powerful AI models. Bloomberg It did not need anything sophisticated. Anthropic said the models got in through weak passwords and systems left open without a login. The company found three incidents after reviewing 141,006 test runs, a check it began after OpenAI said on July 21 that several of its models had broken out of a locked-down test and reached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face. The earliest Claude incident happened in April.

Advertisement

Related Article Cybersecurity AI broke out of its cage and hacked a company. The grid could be next In each test, the model was set the same exercise: break into another machine and retrieve a piece of hidden information. The tests were run with an outside contractor, Irregular. In the first case, the made-up company which Claude had been told to attack shared its name with a real website. Unable to reach the fake target, the model went after the real one and got hold of passwords and a database holding several hundred records of real business data. Anthropic called it the most serious of the three, and the only one where a model kept going after working out the target was real. In the second, Claude found a note inside the practice environment telling staff to download a piece of software that did not exist. So it wrote its own booby-trapped version, set up an email address and an account, and uploaded it to a public library used by programmers worldwide. It sat there for about an hour and was downloaded onto 15 real computers. One belonged to a security firm that automatically installs new software to check it for viruses, which let Claude’s code steal that firm’s passwords and reach further into its systems. The model’s own written reasoning shows it saw the danger. If this were the real internet, it noted, publishing the software would be “NOT okay, and surely not the intended solution”. It then talked itself into believing the whole thing was staged and so carried on.

Advertisement

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. Bloomberg A third model, an experimental version never released to the public, scanned about 9000 possible targets and broke into one company’s website before it realised the system was real and stopped. Related Article Exclusive

AI ChatGPT’s evil twin: How criminals and extremists are using AI to lay traps Anthropic said none of the models tried to escape or chase goals of its own, and that the protections built into the versions of Claude that the public uses would have blocked all of it. The company was contacted for further comment. It has stopped running hacking tests that can reach the internet. Ian Rogers, a former Apple executive now working on AI security at digital security company Ledger, said the incident was a preview. “This happened in one of the world’s best-resourced AI labs,” he said. “Soon, there will be millions of AI agents connected to our email, calendars, financial accounts and enterprise systems.”

Advertisement

The three companies were told on July 27, and two had no idea they had been hacked. Irregular said its investigation was continuing and that it appreciated Anthropic’s “collaboration and transparency”. Related Article AI Silicon Valley’s AI spending spree comes with an Australian invoice Liming Zhu, a CSIRO research director working with the Australian AI Safety Institute on the problem, said the setup error explained most of what happened but not all of it. A well-behaved system should turn cautious when the evidence stops matching its instructions, he said, and the model that kept going after working out the target was real showed poor judgement under pressure. He was warier about treating the newest model’s decision to stop as progress, calling it “an encouraging observation, not an established trend”. It had still scanned thousands of systems and broken into one before it pulled up. The bigger issue for Australian businesses, Zhu said, is that ordinary AI assistants sold for everyday work keep the same hacking abilities under the bonnet. A badly worded instruction or too much system access can bring them out.

Advertisement

Pre-release safety testing is the main check on what frontier models can do before they reach the public, and governments, including Australia’s, are weighing how far to rely on that self-testing. After the OpenAI breach, the Australian Signals Directorate issued a public warning saying that the case showed what powerful AI systems will soon be capable of, and the new Australian AI Safety Institute briefed federal departments. Neither body can compel an AI company to report anything, however. The federal government dropped its plan for mandatory rules covering high-risk AI, and while the European Union and California already require serious AI incidents to be disclosed, Australia does not. Two months ago, Sterling Nasa was sitting in the Sydney audience of La La Land In Concert when Oscar-winning composer-conductor Justin Hurwitz came out after interval to ask if there was an amazing keyboard player in the audience who could take over for a sick musician. The 21-year-old university student, encouraged by his friend Scarlett, stepped up and became the accidental star of the show. “I’ve really got only one shot to give it my best”: Sterling Nasa at the piano. George Chan An incident that sounded like it could have come from the script of La La Land, the musical romance between a jazz musician (played by Ryan Gosling) and an aspiring actress (Emma Stone), went viral around the world. An article in this masthead was followed up by, among many media outlets, The New York Times, The Washington Post, the BBC, The Guardian and CNN. Now Nasa has taken up an invitation by Hurwitz to play piano at La La Land In Concert in Los Angeles – the real La La Land – on Saturday night (Sunday AEST).

Film A musician was too sick to play, so the call went out to the audience. Sterling ran to the stage He will perform at the famous Greek Theatre in Griffith Park, near the landmark observatory that features in the film. “It’s pretty surreal,” Nasa said from his hotel room in Los Angeles. “You’d never think that just going to a concert at [ICC Sydney Theatre] Darling Harbour on Saturday night would lead to getting an opportunity like this. I’m incredibly grateful and I’m stoked.” Nasa, who has been joined by Scarlett on the trip, said he initially thought Hurwitz’s offer “to do a show” meant joining one of the final performances on the Australian tour. “I got on a call with him and he explained that, no, it was a show at the Greek Theatre in LA,” he said. “It’s the 10th anniversary concert and I’m playing the principal piano part.”

Advertisement

In Sydney, Nasa had to play celeste, also known as a bell-piano, for the first time within 90 seconds of arriving on stage. Nervous for the first 10 minutes, he settled to the point of improvising the difficult-to-sight-read synth solo in the John Legend song Start a Fire. He started a fire of his own. Loading “People who I know from places like Nova Scotia, Boston, parts of Scotland were contacting me saying, “Oh, you were in our local newspaper’,” he said. While he has been practising consistently ahead of the Los Angeles concert, Nasa expects to be nervous again.

Advertisement

“It’s a different book from the one I played the other time,” he said. “It’s the piano book, which is a lot harder. I guess there’s some level of expectation this time. “As fun as [Sydney was] – and it was an amazing experience and you wouldn’t change anything – the crowd and the general vibe of the evening really wanted it to work. Now I want to make sure it’s a good performance.” Nasa, who had just finished his final week studying international relations at uni before the Sydney concert, said the accidental performance had made him wonder if he might have a career as a pianist. As well as playing piano at his local church on Sunday mornings, he plays organ and teaches bagpipes at his old school, Scots College. “I’ve certainly seen that there are legitimate opportunities out there,” he said. “I’ve definitely gotten to understand the industry a lot more.” Part of that has been observing Hurwitz behind the scenes.

Advertisement

Backstage selfie after the Sydney concert: Sterling Nasa (right) with Justin Hurwitz. Stirling Nasa “Obviously being a part of it from the get-go and not just from the end of intermission … it shows you how these things work,” he said. “He’s someone who’s very much at the top at the top of his game, and I’d say top of the game as far as Hollywood composers go. “So it’s cool to get to be involved in that [and] very valuable knowledge for someone of my age.” Nasa recognises that, however surreal going from half a show in Darling Harbour to the main piano part in LA seems, he has to play as well as he can for one performance. “I’ve really got only one shot to give it my best,” he said. “I’m the kind of person who just really wants to leave it all out there. So I want to just make sure it’s a good run.”

His hope is that it will be a great experience. “I’m just in it for what I can learn from it,” he said. “If there are to be other opportunities that come from this, I’d be incredibly grateful. [But] it’s a really beautiful thing to come out of what was a very random, coincidental, lovely night that happened in Sydney.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox. title: ‘Tricky, not dishonest’: ICAC witness dodges questions about fake invoices
text:
Advertisement

Follow our live coverage of the ICAC hearing here. NSW Liberal apparatchik and Reformers member Robert Assaf has told a corruption inquiry that fake invoices sent for work that was never carried out were part of a “tricky” tax scheme rather than dishonesty. Assaf, who formed the right-wing Catholic group within the Liberals, on Friday told the Independent Commission Against Corruption that he knew of the “concept” of illegal donations but never thought the Reformers were doing anything wrong in accepting payments, including from hotelier Michael O’Hara. NSW Reformers founder Robert Assaf arrives at ICAC on Friday. James Brickwood The ICAC is probing whether undeclared political donations were made by prohibited donors, including O’Hara, to a company called Beckington. The donations were intended to support the Reformers.

Advertisement

Assaf said he was aware of the “concept” of prohibited donors and knew that some donations to political parties needed to be declared over a threshold, but did not think the Reformers were doing anything wrong. “If someone told me [at] any point before I got my first summons to this, that what I had done was a problem, I would have gone straight to the electoral commission and reported it and sorted it out,” Assaf said. “I can’t recall any time where we discussed ‘are we doing something wrong?’; we never thought that way.” Assaf has told the commission on Friday that O’Hara paid Beckington, rather than the Reformers directly, for “tricky” tax purposes rather than to hide potentially unlawful political donations.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny They claim they didn’t know the rules. So why go to such absurd lengths to hide the cash? Commissioner Fabian Gleeson asked Assaf a “straightforward honesty question”. “I’m asking you to put aside for the moment the question of whether or not it’s appropriate from a tax perspective, do you think it’s honest at the time?” Gleeson asked. “Did you think it was honest for Beckington to issue an invoice claiming money for consultancy services that it said it was providing Mr O’Hara’s company, when in fact no such consultancy services were being provided, as we understand the evidence?” Assaf said he would have thought it was “tricky”.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Analysis

Operation Rosny The self-styled Braveheart crusader now accused of branch stacking “Why do you have a difficulty, Mr Assaf, in distinguishing between tricky and honest conduct?” Gleeson asked. “Why do you characterise them as merely tricky, but you seem to baulk at the characterisation that it’s dishonest conduct by Beckington?” Assaf said he was not aware of how problematic it was, and just thought of it as tricky in an accounting sense. Assaf told the commission that he and other Reformers were “immature and young” and used money from the group as an advance for personal expenditure, which he says they would pay back. In one case, Reformers cash was used to pay for a buck’s party – either for Assaf or Christian Ellis, although he could not remember which since both men got married about the same time.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Jean-Claude Perrottet deserved payment for branch stacking, ICAC hears Senior right-wing MP Damien Tudehope, who has featured heavily in evidence this week through his role in backing the religious group the Reformers, will appear before the commission on Monday. Tudehope has stood aside from Liberal leader Kellie Sloane’s frontbench while the inquiry is under way because of his ties to many of the witnesses. He has denied any wrongdoing and is not a person of interest. On Tuesday, a businessman called Frits Mare will appear. Mare gave explosive evidence to the 2023 parliamentary inquiry into branch stacking in The Hills Shire Council. That inquiry heard Jean-Claude Perrottet and Christian Ellis, both persons of interest in this ICAC inquiry, asked Mare for $50,000 to fund a branch operation to unseat Scott Morrison’s right-hand man Alex Hawke from his federal electorate. Mare wanted no part in their scheme.

The bulk of the week will then be spent hearing from Perrottet, who was a key member of the Reformers. The inquiry heard this week that Perrottet paid for branch memberships and also wanted to be paid for his work stacking branches.
