title: ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects Marc McGowan July 31, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to our first top 30 for this year’s AFL draft class. This is not a mock draft, but rather a ranking of prospects based on performance, potential, injury risk and intangibles, based on discussions with recruiting staff at 10 AFL clubs, junior coaches, and this masthead’s own views. As always, there were players who narrowly missed out, such as Benji van Rooyen, Marlon Neocleous, Koby LeCras, Brady Wright, Albert Macgowan, Jordan Knapp, Anthony Long, Harvey Spawton-Guy, Harvie Cooke and Will Antrobus. The likes of Sebastian Marsic and Sydney Swans academy products Aidan McCartney (also North Melbourne father-son eligible), Mason McGroder – a highly promising long jumper – and Jake Medved are also on clubs’ radar. 1.

Advertisement

Cochrane is yet to play this year because of a knee injury, but will make his return on Sunday for Port Adelaide’s SANFL team, alongside his AFL-listed brother Tom. The AFL approved the Power’s request in November for the super prospect – who can just about play anywhere on the ground – to be draft eligible as part of their Next Generation Academy. Cochrane’s been regarded as the top prospect in the 2026 draft class since he dominated the under-16s championships. He is a great athlete, marks the ball well, is an excellent kick, makes smart decisions and should end up as a goalkicking midfielder and genuine difference-maker. 2. Butler could be the first player picked who is not tied to an AFL club – and might be the most talented prospect in the pool. His kicking skills are peerless, including executing kicks that others cannot, and his athleticism, forward craft, marking ability and nose for the goals make him a constant threat in attack. The main on-field query is Butler’s running capacity, which may limit his ability to play in the midfield. A broken collarbone cut short his championships, and it is unclear when he will next play. Butler’s grandfather, Allan Davis, played in St Kilda’s 1966 flag.

Advertisement

3. Van Hattum is in the Sean Darcy mould as a hulking big man, but more athletic and skilled, which is why he is so coveted. His kicking skills are rare for a ruckman and his follow-up work is Brodie Grundy-like. That said, there is still some nervousness about using such a high selection on Van Hattum. Recruiters would love to see him mark the ball more, particularly as a down-the-line option, and don’t believe he is as athletic as Nic Naitanui, Luke Jackson or Cooper Duff-Tytler. Some scouts are glad they won’t have to make the call on Van Hattum, but the upside is enormous. 4. Gus Teixeira

Advertisement

There is so much to like about “Tex”, who is likened to Adelaide’s Josh Rachele. He lights up games with his power and creativity, and generates scoring opportunities with his penetrating kicking inside 50. Footballers who can make an impact both in attack and the midfield are prized in the AFL, and that is what Teixeira projects to be, particularly if he improves his endurance. His GPS numbers suggest he is not there yet, and explain why he doesn’t have as many prolific games as others – but he could be a match-winner in short order. 5. This is lower than Walker’s name appears on most of these lists, and the extreme likelihood is the Blues will need to match a bid at No.2. The son of Andrew – the second pick in the 2003 draft – is a good size, competitive, combative, powerful, finds the Sherrin easily and can run all day, so there are plenty of high-end traits that will ensure he is a long-term fixture in Carlton’s midfield. However, Walker’s kicking and decision-making will determine how effective and damaging he is at AFL level – and both are question marks at this stage. 6.

Advertisement

This might not be high enough. Drever has carried a titanic load and been ultra-consistent for the Rebels in the Talent League, and impressed again throughout the championships, outside Country’s disappointing performance against Metro. He is a big midfielder who impacts the game inside and outside the contest, can tuck the ball under his arm and burst away, or get it to his boot quickly, but, like Cody Walker, needs to tidy up his kicking at times, including around goal. Drever’s high-end character only adds to his value. 7. Don’t be surprised if Matthews attracts a top-five bid – he is that good. A foot injury meant Matthews appeared just twice at the championships, but he made his mark, particularly with his 35-disposal binge against Vic Country. He is a certain top-10 selection and has racked up possessions for fun all season, averaging 35 touches in the Talent League and not looking out of place in a VFL appearance, either. Matthews is a gut runner, makes quick and generally good decisions, and drives the Sherrin forward at every opportunity off his reliable left boot.

Advertisement

8. Mellody has fans inside the top five, but probably lands in the second half of the top 10 on draft night. He transformed his reputation with a blistering championships display that scored him the Larke Medal as the best-performed player. Mellody was previously pigeonholed as someone who could play on the wing or at half-back as a receiver with silky skills, but his midfield performances for WA blew that out of the water. He swung games when he went in there, and could be in the frame for West Coast’s top pick. 9. Wil Malady

Advertisement

It is all about the upside with Malady, whose “wow” moments are as exciting as anyone in this draft. His aerial prowess is eye-catching, but he isn’t a big ball-winner, so now recruiters are watching to see if the consistent impact follows in the backend of the season. Malady played as a rangy forward and on the wing for Country, but some think he could also be effective as an interceptor. He projects as a third tall in attack at AFL level. There will be some risk with picking Malady, but his potential should be too tempting for him to fall much further than this. 10. Clancy Snell Snell is the consensus best key defender in this class, although some have Mitch Harris ahead of him. His championships left questions on his lockdown defending, although he was regularly under siege in Country’s backline. Snell’s intercepting talents are undoubted, he is good enough athletically, an ideal size, and a good kick. A key defender-needy club might grab him earlier than this, but there could be at least three tall defenders selected in the first round, including Tyson Bradley, so there is depth at the position this year. 11. Caylen Murray (Brisbane Lions academy)

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘It’s been a real challenge for Bobby:’ Pies part ways with flag hero in sad circumstances Brisbane Lions Academy/Allies

Defender/midfielder, 181cm

DOB: 16/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 24 disposals, 5 rebound 50s, 5.5 contested possessions Not everyone rates Murray this highly, but he could attract a top-10 bid, which would make it difficult, or even unlikely, for the Lions to match. His stocks improved at the championships, in part thanks to his positional versatility, but also his numerous AFL traits, as he became the Allies’ sole All-Australian. Murray was a strong performer down back, where he turned defence into offence with his marking, kicking skills, dare – including one triple-bounce effort – agility and pace. He also kicked two goals against South Australia after going forward. 12. Mitch Harris Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

Key defender, 196cm

DOB: 1/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 8.8 disposals, 5 contested possessions, 1.5 intercept marks

Advertisement

Unlike last year’s draft, where Carlton’s Harry Dean was a clear standout, there are options for clubs wanting a high-end key defender. Harris is arguably the best one-on-one defender in it, and often compared to combative Gold Coast backman Sam Collins. He does not offer the same offensive value as Snell, but that doesn’t bother most scouts, given his lockdown proficiency and marking ability at a priority position. Harris might last slightly longer than this, but it is difficult to imagine him slipping outside the top 15. 13. Leo Steed Swan Districts/Western Australia

Midfielder, 177cm

DOB: 7/3/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 23.5 disposals, 10.3 contested possessions, 4.3 clearances Good luck finding someone who doesn’t like or rate Steed. He might not have the highest ceiling among the 2026 draft prospects, but is ultra-professional, a hard worker and thrives in the contest, where his toughness, fast feet and handballing come to the fore. Steed will start at half-forward in the AFL, but should eventually challenge for a midfield spot. You can’t have three players of his stature in the same midfield, but he is driven enough to find his niche. Lachie Neale has helped change opinions on sub-180-centimetre onballers. Leo Steed in action for WA at the championships. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Advertisement

14. Jake Eime Central District/South Australia

Defender, 183cm

DOB: 29/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 20.3 disposals, 4.5 rebound 50s, 3.3 intercept possessions Eime’s draft range starts about here through to the mid-20s, in what is an even section of the draft. He turned heads and changed some opinions on him, particularly with his competitiveness, with a stellar under-18 carnival down back for the South Australians. Eime wants the Sherrin in his hands (he regularly took the kick-ins), takes the game on – whether using his speed or mixing in a sidestep – and has improved his kicking, although it can be tested under pressure. He might need to reduce his risk-taking in the AFL, but that is part of his appeal. 15. Jack Pickett Jack Pickett is tackled during an AFL Futures match last year. via Getty Images

Advertisement

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Key forward, 193cm

DOB: 6/3/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 5 disposals, 3 marks, 2 goals This is an aggressive ranking, and there are recruiters who have him closer to 20 because of the risk involved in drafting someone off an ACL and MCL rupture – but he was in top-five contention pre-setback. The season-ending injury happened innocuously at a Falcons training session after he kicked two goals in the first round of the Talent League. Pickett had everyone’s attention from a bottom-age year when he booted 31 goals in eight matches. He is difficult to stop, whether charging forward on a lead or standing under a high ball in a pack. 16. Sam Gayfer Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Key forward, 194cm

DOB: 21/5/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 11 disposals, 2.5 goals, 7.5 score involvements It will be interesting to see whether Pickett or Gayfer is off the board first. The nephew of Collingwood premiership defender Mick does not come with the same injury risk, which is why some scouts think he is the safer option. Gayfer enjoyed a good championships, kicking four goals against South Australia before three more – all by quarter-time – in Metro’s huge win over Country. He isn’t as athletic as others, but thrives on the physical stuff, including crashing packs and standing his ground under skied passes.

Advertisement

17. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) Western Jets/Vic Metro

Forward, 176cm

DOB: 4/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 10 disposals, 5 tackles, 1 goal Khaled El Souki completes the 20m sprint test. AFL Photos via Getty Images A broken ankle sustained before the championships meant El Souki’s sole appearance was in Metro’s landslide victory over Country. He might not have been prolific, but he hit the scoreboard and made his mark with defensive pressure, including some bruising tackles. El Souki is powerful and typically a goalkicking machine, who has averaged 18 disposals and three goals in the Talent League this season. He would be a wonderful fit in the Bulldogs’ forward line, but they might not be able to match a bid if they trade for Port Adelaide star Zak Butters. 18. Noah Williams

Advertisement

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Midfielder/defender, 176cm

DOB: 22/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 15.5 disposals, 5.3 contested possessions, 3.3 intercept possessions Williams was once touted as a potential top-10 selection, but is no longer certain to be a first-round pick. There is a query on whether he can be a midfielder at AFL level, meaning he might need to make it as a defender or pressure forward. He is fast, aggressive, competitive, works hard, and his kicking can be very good, but is also scrappy at times. Williams’ championships performances left recruiters wanting to see more, so he needs a strong finish to the year to reassert himself. 19. Kodah Edwards South Adelaide/South Australia

Midfielder/forward, 184cm

DOB: 25/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 22 disposals, 3.8 clearances, 7.3 score involvements Edwards is a polarising prospect with a wide draft range that could see him drift a bit at the draft. South Australia’s captain has admirers, can play through the midfield and up forward, thrives in contested situations, and performed well in his senior debut this year for South Adelaide. But he is not as good a runner – the biggest and most common knock on him – or as athletic as other midfielders in the first-round mix. Edwards will likely start as a forward in the AFL, and still has a bit to prove on how transferable his skillset will be.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The 39 minutes that showed why the Cats have the wood over the Pies 20. Toby Krasna Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Wingman, 181cm

DOB: 28/2/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 19 disposals, 3.7 inside 50s, 1 goal Krasna was one of the biggest risers out of the championships. He may end up being taken slightly after this, but comfortably sits in the top 30. Krasna makes quick decisions when necessary, is composed under pressure, tough to tackle with his nimble footwork, and might only be slight, but is willing to wear contact. He kicks the ball well and creatively, and slotted a goal in all three of his matches at the carnival, which was another tick for him. Krasna sat out the last match with hamstring soreness. 21. Harrison Chapman

Advertisement

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

Wingman, 190cm

DOB: 6/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 18.7 disposals, 3 inside 50s, 6.7 score involvements Chapman is another with a wide draft range that starts far earlier than this, but ends significantly lower. He is a great size and beautiful mover who saved his best match of the championships for last with 18 disposals, a goal and nine score involvements in Metro’s comfortable win over Country. Chapman could end up well inside the top 20 if he produces more games like that in the months ahead, but is yet to prove he can consistently do that. Scouts would also like to see him be cleaner and more competitive in the contest and improve his ball security. 22. Tyson Bradley Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Key defender, 196cm

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 14.5 disposals, 5 rebound 50s, 3.3 intercept marks Bradley won Metro’s MVP award after a consistent campaign that put him in first-round contention and among the top group of tall defenders with Clancy Snell and Mitch Harris. He is regarded as a high IQ backman, gobbles up intercept marks and is already physically developed. However, Bradley is not quick and limited athletically, including with his lateral movement, which could leave him vulnerable against the AFL’s best forwards. His smarts help make up for that, and he is compared to Jacob Weitering and Tom Barrass for his defensive craft.

Advertisement

23. Jack Slattery Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

Key forward, 192cm

DOB: 27/9/2007

U18 champs stats (averages): 11.3 disposals, 4.3 marks, 4 goals Slattery bolted up draft boards with an outstanding championships where his 16 goals led everyone. He was overlooked in last year’s draft and turns 19 in September, so that needs to be baked into his performance – but he could hardly have done more. Slattery showed off his set-shot proficiency with a series of brilliant finishes from all angles in a six-goal explosion against the Allies, opportunistically added five more versus Metro, then snapped two beauties from four majors at Country’s expense. Recruiters want to see him play in the Eagles’ senior side down the stretch. 24. Lochie Burrows Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Utility, 181cm

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 13.5 disposals, 4 intercept possessions, 4 score involvements

Advertisement

There is some projection required here because Burrows’ raw numbers – even in the Talent League – don’t jump off the page, but he has many of the physical gifts and traits to be an impact player at AFL level. He leaves opponents in the dust with his acceleration, uses his pace effectively, is elusive in traffic, can play at either end or through the midfield, makes quick decisions – particularly by hand – and kicks the ball well. Burrows could end up being a weapon as a high half-forward, where his speed and marking prowess make him dangerous. 25. Ethan Herbert North Adelaide/South Australia

Ruckman, 201cm

DOB: 1/11/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 15.8 disposals, 10.8 contested possessions, 6 clearances Ethan Herbert (left) and Wil Dawson compete in an AFL national academy match. via Getty Images There are recruiters who won’t consider Herbert in this range due to doubts about his role at the highest level, but he may also go earlier. AFL coaches are increasingly turning to giants near or beyond 210 centimetres to ruck for them, so the centre bounce will be Herbert’s greatest challenge. South Australia mainly operated with Jobe Janeway as its No.1 big man, leaving Herbert to show scouts how he can fare elsewhere. His ground-ball work, clean skills and athleticism help make him an extra midfielder, while some scouts feel he could be a key defender.

Advertisement

26. George Dimer Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Forward, 173cm

DOB: 21/6/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 16 disposals, 8.7 score involvements, 3.3 tackles Dimer’s stature won’t help his cause, but his excellent championships propelled him into top-30 contention, although some view him as a later pick. He is suited to the modern game with his combination of speed, endurance and general athleticism, while he routinely reads the play quicker than his opponents. Dimer might not be a massive goalkicker himself, but has generated so many scoring opportunities this year, whether at the championships, in the Talent League or captaining Haileybury College in school footy. The next Gryan Miers? 27. Jackson Phillips Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

Midfielder/wingman, 184cm

DOB: 30/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 16.3 disposals, 3.3 inside 50s, 3.3 tackles

Advertisement

Phillips spent most of the championships on a wing, which frustrated some recruiters hoping to see how he would go in an inside role. He is a skilful player, highlighted by a slick left-handed pick-up before drilling a goal on the run from 50 metres against Western Australia, but he also missed targets at times going inside 50. Phillips has improved his contest work this year, but still has work to do in that area, and he will be keen to finish the year strongly to solidify his reputation. 28. George Gale Claremont/Western Australia

Midfielder, 190cm

DOB: 6/9/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 27.8 disposals, 9 contested possessions, 3 clearances You can’t argue with Gale’s performance or professionalism, but there are doubts about how much his lack of speed will hold him back in the AFL, which could cause him to slide beyond this. One scout described him as a “poor man’s Steele Sidebottom”, which was meant as a nod to Gale’s football IQ, while acknowledging his ball use is not at the Collingwood star’s level. He is not as damaging with his disposals or movement as the top midfielders in this draft, but scouts want to see him playing senior WAFL football to assess him better. 29. Gabe Patterson

Advertisement

Glenelg/South Australia

Forward, 185cm

DOB: 26/3/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 13 disposals, 7.5 contested possessions, 1 goal In an even crop, Patterson – who was considered a potential top-10 pick at stages last year – just sneaks in on potential despite not having the season he would have liked so far. The tide might be turning, with the athletic forward kicking three goals against Western Australia before returning to Glenelg with a bang post-championships with five goals, including one outrageous checkside finish on the run from the pocket. It is those flashes of skill and athleticism that make him such an intriguing prospect. 30. Xavier Ladbrook Xavier Ladbrook was best on ground in the AFL national academy match. via Getty Images Gippsland Power/Vic Country

Key defender/forward, 201cm

DOB: 16/10/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 16.3 disposals, 3.8 marks, 3.3 tackles

Advertisement

There might not be a harder player to place, given the wide-ranging views on Ladbrook, whose finish to the season will determine whether this ranking is too high, too low or about right. He spent most of his time up forward in the championships, but his best football has come as a defender. That said, Ladbrook has shown glimpses as a forward, too, so it might come down to the eye of the beholder. He is a superb athlete who marks the ball well, so the upside is obvious, but not everyone trusts him. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country. title: ‘A life fully lived’: Rock journalist and cultural commentator, Glenn A. Baker, dies aged 74
text:
Advertisement

Glenn A. Baker, an Australian rock music journalist, collector, commentator, author and broadcaster, has died. He was 74. A long-time contributor to the Herald and The Age, Baker died of old age on Friday morning, his son Orson told this masthead. Glenn A. Baker among his 50,000 records in the Penrith warehouse in 2024. Louise Kennerley “Glenn had an amazing life,” Orson said. “He was so deeply involved in the music industry that we are talking about a man who absolutely had a life fully lived.” He told the ABC earlier that Baker had experienced a “period of illness” and was “declining for a while”.

Advertisement

Born in 1952, Baker grew up in Sydney and Canberra, his love for rock music sparked when at age 12 when he saw evening news coverage of The Beatles arriving at Mascot Airport for their 1964 Australian tour. “Just seeing them, hearing a burst of their music, changed my view of everything, and even though I couldn’t afford to buy the records, I could walk into a record shop and actually touch the brown Parlophone sleeves, which also carried releases by The Easybeats and The Hollies,” Baker told Peter FitzSimons in 2024. A portrait of Baker by artist Nafisa Naomi won the Packing Room Prize in the 2010 Archibald Prize. Getty Baker often credited his long career in music journalism to the first time he heard Bob Dylan’s Like A Rolling Stone a year later. He would recall this moment as an epiphany, whereupon hearing Dylan’s lyrics, Baker decided to dedicate his own life to words. title: ‘Not my signature’: Anytime Fitness probes false signatures on contracts
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive BusinessCompaniesConsumer rights ‘Not my signature’: Anytime Fitness probes false signatures on contracts Elias Visontay July 31, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anytime Fitness has apologised over a string of incidents in which customers were signed up to branches with false signatures inserted into contracts they’d never seen, while others were made to sign blank agreements before terms of their memberships were added. New customers attempting to join Anytime Fitness centres in NSW and Queensland have lodged separate complaints this week about contracting practices at the gym franchise, which has more than 780,000 members across more than 600 premises in Australia. Michael Fraser’s fake signature. Anytime Fitness is investigating after customers’ signatures were falsified and inserted into contracts the clients had never seen. Matt Willis Michael Fraser had been growing dissatisfied with his longtime gym on the Gold Coast when, in mid-June, he inquired with a soon-to-launch Anytime Fitness in the suburb of Biggera Waters, a more convenient location for him. He was offered a discounted rate over the phone and broadly agreed to the offer. Fraser was asked to leave his payment details with the club to reserve the terms as an inaugural member of the gym.

Advertisement

He was told that when the branch finally opened, he could go into the gym, show his ID, complete an orientation and pre-exercise questionnaire, before reading and signing a contract outlining his membership terms. But on Tuesday, an email landed in his inbox claiming his membership had started, and his signed contract was attached, despite Fraser having had no further direct dealings with the gym. The false signature, which mimicked handwriting, appeared three times throughout the contract, which included terms he felt were not reflected in the initial phone call he’d had with the gym. It resembled the template signatures available in common contract-management software. “I just knew it wasn’t my signature, I don’t put dots between my initials,” Fraser said. His colleague, Maddison Johnstone, who had also given her details, keen to sign up when the gym opened, similarly received an email about 24 hours later with a contract containing signatures that were not hers.

Advertisement

“I have never been sent an unsigned copy, and have never read or even sighted it. I never provided my signature, digital or otherwise,” said Johnstone, who was also surprised the length of the contract was 18 months. “It is something I would never have signed.” Related Article Consumer rights Gyms push back on law change that would ease cancellation “The gym isn’t open yet, so I am not sure how four weeks free starting yesterday makes sense,” Johnstone said. Fraser and Johnstone are co-founders of Operation Redress, a consumer advocacy firm which has raised whistleblower concerns to push for reforms of systemic issues of laws governing franchise businesses. Fraser’s advocacy has included raising concerns surrounding what became a major wage fraud scandal for 7/11. After Fraser aired a complaint about his experiences, Anytime Fitness launched an investigation. Its Australian chief executive, Simon Thompson, called Fraser directly on Wednesday.

Advertisement

An Anytime Fitness spokeswoman confirmed it had begun an internal investigation into the contracts. “Given the serious nature of this matter, we are reviewing all relevant documentation, systems, and processes to establish the facts,” they said. Fraser and Johnstone’s experience is similar but separate to what Rachel Sarfatij alleges happened to her when signing up for the Anytime Fitness branch in the Sydney suburb of Randwick. She had been going to a Fitness First but in an inconvenient location, and was wooed by a $6-per-week-for-six-weeks deal at Anytime. “I went in, talked to them, got the spiel, agreed on a price and a year time frame.” Sarfatij mentioned that she lived close to another Anytime location, and may visit that branch more, something the employee said would not be an issue.

Advertisement

She was then handed an iPad and asked to sign on a screen in which only the signature box, and not the rest of the contract, was visible.“I couldn’t see anything that I was signing, but I figured we had just verbally agreed on the terms, what else were they going to do?” Immediately after signing, Sarfatij claims the employee then told her that if she went to another branch more frequently than the Randwick one, her membership would automatically shift there and she’d have to pay different fees. She was also made to pay $69.95 for an electronic key fob to enter the gym. When Sarfatij received the full contract via email, all the boxes that normally outline the details of a membership were unpopulated. Outside of her signature, the contract was essentially blank. After a back and forth, Sarfatij said the gym manager admitted there was a technical issue, and Sarfatij asked to cancel her contract, which was within a seven-day cooling-off period.

Advertisement

“I had such a bad feeling in my stomach, I don’t trust being stuck in a contract with this gym,” she said. Related Article Home loans Home owners warned to check offset accounts after $55 million interest issue But the manager emailed Sarfatij to refuse to return the almost $70 she had paid for the key. “As outlined in the membership agreement you signed, the key fob fee is non-refundable,” the manager wrote. Citing a term in a contract the gym admitted Sarfatij never saw infuriated her. “If they admit the mistake with the contract, how can they refuse me a refund?” The Anytime spokeswoman said there had been an intermittent technical issue with the third-party software it uses to populate membership agreements.

Advertisement

“While the technical issue has been resolved, it does not excuse the way the situation was handled … we regret the inconvenience caused,” the spokeswoman said. Sarfatij is yet to a receive a refund. Speaking more broadly on the contract claims, the spokeswoman said: “We certainly take any matter relating to the integrity of our membership processes and the member experience extremely seriously. “It’s disappointing that a situation like this can impact the trust our members, franchisees and club teams have worked hard to build over the past 18 years. That’s why we’ll take every necessary step to investigate thoroughly, establish the facts, and take action where appropriate,” the spokeswoman said. title: 'Grotesque': Football world in revolt against FIFA's controversial World Cup plan
text:
In brief European football's governing body UEFA said it would boycott the World Cup if FIFA's privatisation proceeds.

Football Australia has asked for more time to consider the proposal.

European football's governing body UEFA has said it would boycott the World Cup if FIFA pressed ahead with a controversial private investor plan.

"No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership," UEFA said in a statement released on Friday.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product ... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale."

On Tuesday, football's world governing body FIFA announced plans to create a commercial subsidiary to run its biggest events, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

Under the proposal, private investors would be allowed to acquire stakes in the company but would remain minority shareholders, FIFA said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It hopes to raise up to US$4.2 billion ($5.9 billion) based on a valuation of US$20 billion ($28 billion) for the FIFA Forward Enterprise initiative.

If approved, the project could provide each of FIFA's 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027 and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million ($11.3 million) to US$20 million ($28 million).

FIFA president Gianni Infantino described the initiative on Wednesday as a "golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally".

But UEFA, whose president Aleksander Čeferin boycotted the World Cup final to show unhappiness with FIFA, argued: "This model has no place in world football.

"Football's future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return.

"Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain," Čeferin said.

"Europe's position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No-one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation."

The FIFA proposal has drawn criticism from not only UEFA but also several leading European federations and European Union officials, who view it as another step in the commercialisation of sport and have raised concerns over potential conflicts of interest.

The EU praised UEFA on Thursday for "defending the integrity of the game".

"I welcome this UEFA statement and fully support its position," European commissioner for sports Glenn Micallef said in a social media post.

"Proud to see Europe's football associations leading on governance, standing firm on their principles," he posted.

The 41 members of the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF), including the three co-hosts of the recent World Cup — the United States, Mexico and Canada — unanimously rejected the proposal on Friday.

North and Central American football's governing body said its members "expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies".

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) also expressed concern that the FIFA proposal was made public before all 211 member associations were fully consulted.

The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has urged its members to review FIFA's divisive plan.

Never for sale

UEFA said in its statement Thursday that the World Cup was "one of football's greatest sporting legacies ... built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game," UEFA said.

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football.

"National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum — accept the irreversible capture of football's greatest competitions or bear the consequences.

"This is not a 'democratic decision' but governance by intimidation — an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game."

UEFA added: "There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept but by what they refuse to compromise. This is one of those moments.

"Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale."

On Tuesday, newly installed British Prime Minister Andy Burnham hit out at FIFA's plan.

"Let me say this very directly," Burnham wrote in a statement on X. "Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine."

Football Australia considers its options

Football Australia was unmoved by the growing global pushback against FIFA's plans, telling media that it had received FIFA's plans but wanted more time to consider the proposal.

"We have requested further information from Fifa to properly assess the strategic, commercial, and governance implications of such a significant step," a spokesperson told The Guardian.

"We will only be able to form a position after receiving this information and engaging in further dialogue with our peer member associations and our confederation."

Professional Footballers Australia, which serves as the Australian players' union and represents both the Socceroos and the Matildas, said that "these tournaments should not be for sale."

"If accepted, it would open the door to the privatisation of FIFA World Cups and other FIFA competitions," PFA chief executive Beau Busch told ESPN.

"The PFA is disturbed by the lack of transparency surrounding the proposal and the absence of meaningful consultation with those that generate the value that FIFA is seeking to exploit — the players and the fans."

In a statement released on Wednesday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), in which Football Australia sits, said it had not been consulted by FIFA about the FIFA Forward Enterprise initiative and expressed disappointment with the lack of transparency.

It did not, however, condemn FIFA's plans outright.

"The AFC firmly believes that all stakeholders should be provided with sufficient information and adequate time to assess the proposal in full, including its governance, legal, commercial and strategic implications. Such a process is essential to ensuring that any decision reflects the collective interests of the global football community and reinforces confidence in FIFA's governance framework."

New Zealand Football and the Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) felt similarly.

Others in the Australian football sphere were not quite as reserved.

"It will fall on the players, current and former, and fans around the world to protect their World Cup. For future generations," said former Socceroo Craig Foster.

Liberal senator Dave Sharma called the proposal "grotesque", saying that he believed the World Cup should not be privatised.

"It is clear from the reaction of Football Australia and other regional confederations and associations that they have been blindsided by this proposal.

"The fact that a change of this significance was announced without any meaningful prior engagement or consultation only adds to the suspicion surrounding it."

title: The visiting stars who will have to fill out the 2026 Census
text:
IN BRIEF The Census is compulsory for everyone who will be in Australia on 11 August, including visiting international stars.

The form must be completed in English, but information and resources are available in different languages.

On Tuesday 11 August, Italian footballing history will be made as Juventus and Palermo FC face off in Perth as part of the Calcio Italiano tournament.

That same night, players will also partake in a distinctly Australian tradition — the Census of Population and Housing.

The survey is conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) every five years. It's designed to capture and count every person in the country on Census night.

That includes international visitors, such as the Piedmont-based Juventus and the Sicilian-based Palermo football teams, who will be competing in the Australian pre-season football tournament for the first time.

Palermo FC CEO Giovanni Gardini described the upcoming Calcio Italiano tournament in Western Australia as a "historic opportunity". Source: Getty / Gabriele Maricchiolo

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Female footballers from Chelsea FC Women will also be in Australia ahead of the final match of the Sydney Super Cup on 12 August.

It's not just sports stars; English trip-hop collective Massive Attack are set to perform at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on Census night. German-French cellist Nicolas Altstaedt and French lutenist Thomas Dunford will be hosting a masterclass in Melbourne that same day.

United States actors Zac Efron, Kate Walsh, and supermodel Tyra Banks are among the international celebrities who have reportedly relocated to Australia in recent years. Meanwhile, Punjabi rapper and songwriter Karan Aujla is set to perform in Perth on 13 August.

SBS News has been unable to independently verify the whereabouts of any of these people on Census night. However, anyone in the country on 11 August is expected to complete the Census.

Why is everyone counted in the Census?

Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University's Centre for Social Policy Research, said the Census is deliberately designed to provide a broad snapshot of the nation.

"It gives us an important reference point of who's in the country at that particular time," she told SBS News.

The Census is compulsory for all Australians, international visitors, temporary residents, migrants and refugees in the country. However, Australians who are overseas on 11 August do not complete the Census.

Generally, one person completes the form on behalf of their household.

Allen said that allows the ABS to collect information on "who might be staying over at a friend's house or gran's house" on Census night.

"So it's not just a Census of people. It's a Census of Population and Housing. It gives us essential information on ... how and where we live and then housing stock in the country."

The Census is usually completed online; however, individual and paper forms can be requested if preferred.

How can international visitors and students complete Census?

For international visitors and students staying in hotels, motels or student accommodation, instructions on how to complete the Census will be provided by accommodation staff.

Paper forms should be available at locations including bed and breakfasts, cruise ships, commercial vessels and snowfield accommodation.

More than 61,000 overseas visitors were counted in the 2021 Census amid the COVID-19 pandemic, compared to around 315,000 in 2016. Source: AP / Mark Baker

International visitors staying in holiday rental properties (such as Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with free internet access.

People staying in remote locations or free camping sites can visit Accredited Visitor Information Centres to access Census forms. The completed survey can be mailed via the provided Reply Paid envelope.

All details, including personal information collected during the Census, are strictly confidential and protected by law. The Census must be completed in English.

Jenny Telford, general manager of the Census and Population division at the ABS, said resources are available for people whose first language is not English.

"We have our translation and interpreting service available that anybody can call if they need in language assistance," she told SBS News.

"We're also planning fill-in form centres and pop-up hubs across the country, which are physical places that people can go to get the assistance that they need to participate."

Online information about the Census, including information for people visiting or travelling from overseas, is available in 26 languages.

title: The Pacific nation caught between two superpowers
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Amid escalating rivalry between the United States and China, a pristine paradise in the western Pacific is confronting what it means to be part of the "tip of America's spear" in the region.

Home to around 18,000 people, the nation of Palau is comprised of hundreds of tiny, uninhabited, volcanic islands jutting out of the surrounding ocean. The archipelago is covered in lush vegetation and surrounded by turquoise lagoons and coral reefs.

The distinctive limestone islands that make the nation such an international drawcard are just a short walk from 18-year-old Dior Imaim Ngiraboi's home.

The recent high school graduate has fond memories growing up here, swimming in the crystal-clear water and playing in the nearby forest. Like so many Palauans, Ngiraboi has a deeply personal and cultural connection to the natural environment.

She meets SBS News at the water's edge on a typically warm morning. A few street dogs have risen from their slumber, watching with curiosity. It's here that Ngiraboi tells us about the traditional conservation concept of 'bul'.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It's a very, very big part of Palauan culture," she says.

"It's something our ancestors knew was a necessity, to allow our environment to heal, to be able to continue providing for us. Growing up, we were told to take care of the environment because it's taking care of us."

Dior Imaim Ngiraboi is one of seven Palauan students who filed complaints with the United Nations challenging US military expansion in Palau. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

For Ngiraboi, that connection to the land is being reshaped by a changing strategic reality in the region.

Amid growing rivalry with China, the US has expanded its military footprint across these islands, and many Palauans are balancing hopes for greater security with concerns about the environmental, cultural and social costs.

In late 2024, Ngiraboi was among seven Palauan high school students who filed a complaint to two United Nations Special Rapporteurs. The complaint alleged the expansion of the US military presence in Palau was harming local communities and the natural environment.

The allegations have not been tested in court. The US says it takes concerns about its projects seriously but broadly disputes the students' claims.

Inside the US military expansion in Palau

The US has been steadily building and revamping military sites across Palau, including World War Two-era runways, naval facilities and sophisticated radar systems.

SBS News visited one of these sites, still under construction, which will eventually become an unmanned Tactical Mobile Over-the-Horizon Radar (TACMOR) transmitter.

According to its Environmental Impact Statement, the 22-hectare facility would "improve the United States' and its regional partners' ability to monitor air and maritime platforms in the vicinity of Palau and vastly beyond the horizon to enhance domain awareness, safety, and security".

The US military declined to provide further details about the site , citing the "sensitivity and special capability of the TACMOR".

The planned radar system in Palau will use over-the-horizon technology to monitor air and maritime activity across a wider area of the Pacific. Source: SBS News

However, the military showed SBS News its planned upgrade of Malakal Port, the main commercial hub serving Koror, Palau's biggest city.

The multi-million-dollar project would expand the port's length to approximately 250 metres, allowing large-scale vessels — including warships — as well as heavy equipment and personnel to move more quickly during times of crisis or regional contingencies.

Relations between Palau and the US are governed by the Compact of Free Association (COFA), a long-standing agreement under which Washington is responsible for Palau's defence and provides significant economic support in exchange for exclusive military access and strategic rights.

Sergeant Major Jimmy Castro, senior enlisted leader of the Joint Task Force - Micronesia, says the US force in Palau is "committed to building regional stability and security for the Pacific region".

"Our partnership with Palau serves as a warning to potential adversaries that any conflict in this region will be a grave miscalculation , " he tells SBS News.

Palau caught in US-China rivalry

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth has described the second island chain — a strategic arc stretching across the western Pacific that includes Palau — as the "tip of America's spear in the Pacific".

The second island chain lies in the middle of the western Pacific. It stretches from mainland Japan, passes through Japan's Bonin Islands, the US territories of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam, extends to Palau and ends in Western New Guinea, Indonesia. Source: SBS News

In May, during a speech to the Shangri-La Dialogue — Asia's premier defence summit held in Singapore — Hegseth warned of "China's historic military buildup" in the region.

The following month, the Palauan government complained to the Chinese government about a Chinese-flagged research vessel that allegedly entered Palau's Exclusive Economic Zone without warning.

The complaint alleged that "the vessel appeared to conduct questionable research-related activities without authorisation, activities that threaten Palau's national security and disregard its sovereignty and rules-based order".

China did not publicly respond to the complaint, but has previously defended similar actions as compliant with international maritime law.

Jodean Remengesau, a Palau-based expert with the Pacific Center for Island Security, says: "It seems like they're testing the waters."

"It's not as aggressive, but they're making their presence known," she tells SBS News.

Jodean Remengesau says the US-China strategic contest will "impact us sooner or later". Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

Remengesau says the strategic competition between the US and China is shaping the security environment across the Pacific, including in Palau.

"We're in an oasis mindset. It seems like things these days are quite peaceful, but it'll impact us sooner or later," she says.

It's almost like the big elephant in the room that no-one wants to acknowledge.

Kambes Kesolei is a veteran Palau-based journalist and founder of the Compass Point Institute, the country's first locally established think tank.

Kambes Kesolei says the scale of US military activity in Palau is unlike anything he has seen since COFA came into effect in 1994. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

Kesolai says he's never seen this level of US military engagement since the COFA entered into force in 1994.

"Every time you put military installations in an area where there's high tension and geopolitical rivalry, you make yourself a target; you're in the crosshairs," Kesolei tells SBS News.

Palau's Taiwan dilemma

Palau is one of just three Pacific Island nations to recognise Taiwan as a sovereign nation.

Across the country, SBS News observed several development projects jointly funded by Taiwan, including the government's main administrative office and its capital building in Ngerulmud.

The Palaun Capitol building in Ngerulmd is among the infrastructure projects jointly funded with support from Taiwan. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

US Army veteran and Palauan resident, Tutii Chilton, says tensions between Beijing and Washington over Taiwan have left Palau "between a rock and a hard place".

"This is not our issue. Palau doesn't have any enemies. Our only enemies are our friends' enemies," he tells SBS News.

Despite having served in the military, Chilton says he now has serious concerns about his country's growing closeness to the US.

"I respect the military, I was a veteran, and I believe in it. And yet, people forget about the target that is put on your back."

US Army veteran and Palauan resident Tutii Chilton says rising geopolitical tensions are forcing Palau to confront difficult questions about its future. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

Chilton says the COFA means Palau has given the US significant responsibility over its defence and strategic affairs.

It's not democracy. It's profits, military expansion to hold on to profits, and businesses. That's the bottom line … it's still colonisation, 2026 style.

The US rejects the suggestion that the relationship is unequal, pointing to the compact's economic benefits, security arrangements and the voluntary service of many Palauans in the US military.

Asked whether he'd describe the relationship as "equal", Castro responds, "absolutely".

"The significance of the US-Palau partnership is definitely based on trust to maintain peace in the Pacific," he says.

The military also points out that Palauans serve in the US military at a higher rate per capita than any other nation, as well as most US states and territories, which it says "speaks volumes" about the relationship.

Former vice-president of Palau, Elias Camsek Chin, is another veteran with the US military. He served for 23 years across multiple continents and says the US presence in Palau has been a force for good.

Former vice-president of Palau, Elias Camsek Chin, says the US presence has helped maintain peace and security in the Pacific. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

"The US has been trying to maintain peace throughout the world for a long, long time , " the 77-year-old tells SBS News.

We don't have any enemies.

"It's the other countries that don't want to be friends with us."

'Deep concerns' from UN rapporteurs

Dior Imaim Ngiraboi and her fellow students submitted their complaint to the UN after interviewing residents across Palau through the community-based NGO Ebiil Society.

She says some residents described the lasting legacy of major World War Two battles, fought by US and Japanese forces on the southern island states of Peleliu and Angaur.

Unexploded ordnance from the conflict remains a safety issue in parts of Palau.

"When the military first came to Palau in World War Two, the damage was irreversible, and you can still see the effects to this day," she says.

"So, if that was then, what will happen now?"

In October, the students received a response from the group of UN-appointed Special Rapporteurs, expressing "deep concern" over reported breaches of Palau's environmental protection laws.

The UN Special Rapporteurs' response was based on the information provided in the complaint and did not constitute a legal finding against the US.

Castro says the military ensures compliance with local laws and environmental requirements.

"There are always concerns and inquiries regarding military construction projects, and we take that very seriously," he says.

But while military construction continues, Ngiraboi's activism goes on.

"I just hope they can take responsibility and proceed more with care, to be more considerate of the people and environment around them.

This is our life. They come to work. But this is our life, this is how we live. I want them to be able to respect it.

title: An issue of trust: The 'worrying' problem Australia faces
text:
IN BRIEF Australians' trust in each other has dropped to a low unseen this decade, with trust in democracy also declining.

Increasing political discourse about multiculturalism and national identity could be behind rising mistrust.

Australia celebrates the value of mateship, but distrust between the population has grown to the highest level reported this decade.

A survey of over 3,500 people, conducted by the Australian National University in June, suggests Australians trust each other less than they did during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Professor Nicholas Biddle, head of ANU's School of Politics and International Relations, said some of the findings were concerning.

"Worryingly, interpersonal trust among Australians has fallen to 5.32 on a scale of 0 to 10 — the lowest value recorded in ANUpoll during the 2020s,'' he said.

"This sits below the pre-COVID value of 5.53 recorded in October 2019 and reverses the increase in trust observed during the pandemic."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Researchers asked participants three questions: whether they believed most people could be trusted, whether someone would take advantage of them if given the chance, and whether people are generally helpful or selfish in their choices.

While the results for all three indicated declining trust, the most dramatic decrease was in belief that others can be trusted, Biddle said.

He also noted that trust remains strongest among "older Australians, degree holders and the employed".

Age, employment and life satisfaction

The findings follow data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ General Social Survey from 2025 that found half of Australians felt others could be trusted — compared to 61 per cent in 2020.

Similarly, Scanlon Foundation Research Institute CEO Anthea Hancocks said the findings reflected those of her organisation.

"People who are employed each day or very often are going to a workplace where there are other people working towards a similar goal — and they're getting paid," she explained.

"That gives you a greater sense of self-worth that you may not necessarily have if you're unemployed."

She suggested that higher trust among older Australians may be related to her organisation's findings that this cohort had "a higher sense of belonging than any other age group".

"That's generally because they know the world in which they're living; they're quite comfortable with their circumstances," she said.

"They know what they are and have an understanding of what the future holds. Unlike young people, whose sense of belonging is way below average."

The ANUpoll also found that between March and June of 2026, life satisfaction in Australia plateaued at 6.22 out of 10.

Over the same period, the proportion of those who experienced difficult or very difficult levels of financial stress decreased slightly from 34.9 per cent in March to 33 per cent in June.

Australians also were found to be more dissatisfied than satisfied with the direction of the nation in 2026, compared with January 2020.

Perceptions of democracy

The survey also found that satisfaction in the way democracy works in Australia fell from 65.7 to 63.8 per cent between March and June this year.

While it's the lowest reported rate since January 2023, in-principle support of democracy increased from 66.9 per cent in May 2025 to 72 per cent in June 2026.

READ MORE Under half of young Australians believe democracy is always a preferable form of government

"Australians are becoming more critical of how democracy is being delivered without withdrawing their commitment to democracy itself," Biddle said.

He said agreement with core democratic norms, such as that no-one should be above the law, remains very high and largely unchanged since March.

Civil debate key to 'positive' change

ANU acting head of psychology professor Michael Platow, who wasn't involved in the study, said "declining trust isn't necessarily bad" — it depends on what else is occurring.

"We trust people we think are part of us in some sense; it's called group membership ... we have a tendency to trust 'us'," he said.

"A lack of trust could mean there's disintegration — where people are not seeing 'us' as all Australians together and seeing 'us' more as subgroups with competing interests."

He believes perceived disintegration could be fuelled by political discourse about multiculturalism and Australian nationalism.

"There are political debates, like it or not, that say some people ... aren't really Australians," he said.

"The psychological construction of 'us' is what is being manipulated through political discourse ... and that can certainly lead to a decrease in overall trust."

Platow said that Australia's broad embrace of multiculturalism enabled a larger understanding of national identity.

"Multiculturalism allowed us to be diverse. It didn't make Australia perfect ... There was still racism and prejudice, but it does form a kind of subjective and psychological basis for 'us' and helped us deal with the diversity that is a reality of our country," he said.

READ MORE A dark chapter of Australia's past is resurfacing in immigration politics

While political debate can disintegrate that notion of 'us', Platow believes it's crucial to "positive social change".

He cited the White Australia Policy as an example, saying this particular form of racial discrimination was ended by Australia "questioning and challenging who we are and what we are".

Build trust in your own backyard

For the many Australians who feel disconnected from political debate and discourse, Hancocks recommends building trust in their own backyard.

"If people live in an area of high neighbourhood cohesion, which would indicate a degree of trust in their neighbourhood, then their level of happiness goes up," she said.

"If your level of happiness goes up, you're somewhat more optimistic about the future because the things around you are giving you some degree of hope."

She said hope and "optimism" about being able to overcome negative circumstances strengthens a person's sense of self and their trust in others.

"You can't force it, and we have to recognise that trust is easily lost and really hard to build. People do have trusted relationships that they're reluctant to let other people into," she said.

"But within local areas, there are lots of community organisations and councils that are doing all sorts of things to try and bring people together and help them connect.

She offered encouragement to people "to step into an area in which they feel comfortable and start to reach out."

title: This drug was the only thing that worked for Kirsten. She's unsure how much longer she'll have it
text:
Ashleigh Middleton has spent months campaigning to keep a drug that's holding her cancer at bay on Australian shelves.

Now she's won — but says the uncertainty surrounding long-term access hasn't gone away.

The 31-year-old breast cancer patient was shocked when it was announced in April that Zoladex — a monthly implant used to suppress hormones in women with hormone-positive breast cancer as well as a range of other conditions affecting women — would be pulled from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and no longer supplied through its usual distribution pathway from 1 November.

The decision, made by the drug's manufacturer, AstraZeneca, prompted concern among patients and clinicians who questioned how those who rely on the treatment would access an alternative and whether suitable substitutes would be available for all conditions the implant is used to treat.

Australia was the only market in the world affected.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Angered by the move and worried about the precedent it could set for other medications, Middleton started a change.org petition, calling on AstraZeneca to reverse the decision and urging the federal government and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee to secure PBS-listed alternatives.

The petition has since attracted more than 42,000 signatures.

Ashleigh Middleton's petition asked AstraZeneca to reverse the decision to pull Zoladex from the Australian market, earning 42,000 signatures. Source: Supplied / Ashleigh Middleton

On 16 July, AstraZeneca reversed course.

The company now says it will provide the monthly implant free of charge to patients who have no suitable alternative, with no end date listed — a shift from its earlier plan to provide six months of free access while patients transitioned to other arrangements.

Asked whether AstraZeneca could guarantee the medication would remain available, a spokesperson told SBS News: "The Zoladex Continuity Program is not a time-bound program."

For Middleton, it's a win worth celebrating — but not one that has settled her nerves.

"It's a really, really good step in the right direction, but it's definitely not all the way there," she tells SBS News.

I think putting in that indefinite timeline does leave it a bit questionable — nobody really knows what that means.

"But I think AstraZeneca have recognised it was probably a bad decision on their part, so at least putting a little something extra in there, saying it's indefinitely going to be available and that there's no cut-off time, I think is a positive," Middleton says.

"But I think the indefinite will definitely run out of time."

Two weeks on from that announcement, with November fast approaching, those affected are left with a mix of celebration, confusion and ongoing concern about what access will look like in practice.

Why patients fear losing access

While many people may not have heard of Zoladex, its 3.6mg implant has become a lifeline for many of the patients who rely on it.

It's prescribed to suppress hormones in premenopausal women with hormone-positive breast cancer, helping reduce the risk of recurrence by suppressing ovarian hormone production.

It's also given to some patients with endometriosis who haven't responded adequately to other treatments. In some cases, it's used to protect ovarian function and preserve fertility in women undergoing chemotherapy, including those whose cancers are not hormone-driven.

The suitability depends on an individual patient's circumstances, and medical specialists determine whether it is the most appropriate treatment option.

In 2025, 13,580 patients were prescribed the medication in Australia.

In its announcement, AstraZeneca committed to supplying the 3.6mg implant "at no cost in Australia from 1 November 2026" for patients without a suitable treatment pathway.

"'Without suitable treatment pathways' means that if the clinician determines there are no suitable alternative treatments for the patient, then they will receive access to the Zoladex monthly (3.6mg) implant through the Zoladex Continuity Program," an AstraZeneca spokesperson tells SBS News.

"Therefore, if a clinician prescribes the implant as a new treatment option for a patient after 1 November 2026, they will be able to receive access to it through the Zoladex Continuity Program."

It's set to apply to patients currently taking the drug and those who may need to start it after that date, across the range of conditions the implant is designed to treat.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing says patients will continue to access the implant through their normal prescribing and dispensing arrangements until 31 October.

AstraZeneca says further advice for healthcare professionals, including details about registration and enrolment, will be released in September.

A second, higher dose — the 10.8mg implant, given every three months — is used to treat prostate cancer in men and is unaffected by the withdrawal.

AstraZeneca has applied to extend the 10.8mg implant's PBS listing to hormone receptor-positive breast cancer patients, but the Therapeutic Goods Administration is still assessing that submission.

AstraZeneca tells SBS News the 10.8mg implant is "registered for use in breast cancer in more than 70 countries" and that they had prepared a submission demonstrating it is "non-inferior" to the monthly dosage for certain types of breast cancer.

Before the reversal, Dr Christine Lai, a general surgeon who treats women with breast cancer, told SBS News the three-monthly dose is "not as efficacious in keeping the hormone levels suppressed in younger women".

She added that similar doubts had been raised about whether it's a viable substitute for endometriosis or fertility preservation at all, conditions Australia would be left to test alone as the only market affected by AstraZeneca's decision.

'It's caused so much stress'

Few people have felt the whiplash more than Kirsten — who, for privacy reasons, doesn't want SBS News to use her last name. She was diagnosed with endometriosis ten years ago but has lived with the condition for much longer.

The 32-year-old tried close to 20 different medications, several surgeries to remove the endometriosis, and a total hysterectomy three years ago to manage her pain and symptoms, leaving just one ovary in place at the recommendation of her specialist.

Zoladex is the only thing to have worked for her. Without access to it, she says her only other option may be surgery to have her remaining ovary removed — a decision she does not want to make without exploring other treatment options with her specialist.

"I'm really happy that endometriosis has been acknowledged in the access period and that it will remain available for me, but I don't know — I'm still concerned that they could change their mind at any time and remove it," Kirsten tells SBS News.

She doesn't fully understand the reasoning behind the reversal.

"If they can afford to offer it for free, then what's the problem with it being on the PBS? It doesn't make any sense whatsoever."

A spokesperson for AstraZeneca earlier told SBS News: "The decision to discontinue the Zoladex monthly [3.6mg] implant from Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme reflects the way the PBS currently works, which means that the price offered is too low, making it unsustainable to supply the medicine on the PBS."

With November fast approaching, Kirsten remains unsure how the enrolment process will work and is worried about whether accessing the program will require additional appointments with gynaecologist — appointments she says can already be difficult to afford.

It's honestly terrifying not knowing what's going to happen.

"I want to be happy that they've opened up the access program, but all of the uncertainty on how it's going to work and whether I'm going to be able to get access from the get-go is so stressful," she says.

"I'm cancelling holidays. I'm making sure that I'm banking leave at work in case I can't get access to medication and start having flare-ups again and can't work."

A spokesperson for AstraZeneca confirmed to SBS News there should be "no difference for patients who need continuous access to the Zoladex monthly implant".

Kirsten says the experience has affected her trust in both AstraZeneca and the government, although she acknowledges the reversal has provided some reassurance.

"All of these decisions seem like they've come out of the blue," she says.

"Especially now with the backflip on the access program — it's caused so much stress and so much uncertainty that I don't know what to believe anymore."

"I don't know what's going to happen. I don't know anything."

'Smoke and mirrors'

Dr Sharmitha Kathurusinghe, a Melbourne gynaecologist who works predominantly with endometriosis patients, welcomed the reversal but says it raises questions about the long-term future of access.

"If it was too unsustainable and a low price to provide it on the PBS, what is motivating AstraZeneca now to provide this free for our patients? And for how long will they do this?" she tells SBS News.

"Is it because of criticism that they have faced in the light of the fact that women will not be able to have this medication?

It is reasonable for us to be concerned that this may just be smoke and mirrors.

"In my experience in gynaecology care, I have not personally seen this happen before."

Kathurusinghe is also concerned about how straightforward the September enrolment process will actually be for patients.

"They might have to jump through more hoops and have multiple people sign paperwork to make it more challenging and not as straightforward to start the medication," she says.

An AstraZeneca spokesperson tells SBS News a patient's clinician will determine the patient's suitability for the prescription, including whether there are suitable alternative treatments.

"Clinicians will need to enrol patients into the Zoladex Continuity Program."

What AstraZeneca says about ongoing access

In a letter seen by SBS News, AstraZeneca's director of Corporate Affairs for Australia and New Zealand, Penny George, referenced Middleton's "coordination of the 42,000+ signatories" to her petition.

Middleton sees the acknowledgement as recognition of the pressure generated by the campaign.

For Middleton, the significance of the past few months extends beyond securing continued access to Zoladex 3.6mg — it is also about demonstrating that patients can influence conversations about medicines they rely on.

"I think the reassuring thing for me is less about the indefinite option of having Zoladex and more about the fact that if we make a lot of noise, they do respond to it," she says.

"I think the anxiety of medications being taken away will probably never go away for people that have had this occur, because it's not fun to go through. But I think it's definitely a step in the right direction at least from AstraZeneca."

She's not shy about crediting the people who pushed for change alongside her.

"The breast cancer community, we're a force.

"So don't mess with us."

READ MORE Breast cancer patients in Australia to save thousands as new drug added to PBS

While allowing herself to celebrate, Middleton is clear-eyed that little here is guaranteed.

"Whenever a company as big as AstraZeneca makes a move like this, it does get that anxiety going," she says.

"I don't think that would particularly go away, especially now that we've seen that they can do it and that these companies are comfortable doing it," she says. "We still haven't gotten approval for the higher dose on the PBS."

Unfortunately, it hasn't brought any more comfort about the future issues with access.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing previously acknowledged the limits of the government's role, telling SBS News that pharmaceutical companies "make their own commercial decisions" and "cannot be compelled by government to continue to list a product on the PBS".

Kirsten, who is waiting for more information, is calculating how much time she has left before the changes take effect.

"This year, it seems like it's absolutely flying by," she says.

"If I look at it in terms of injections, then I've only got two that I'm somewhat guaranteed to be able to access before I'm affected."

Even Middleton, for all her relief, doesn't expect the uncertainty to disappear completely.

"As much as I appreciate the indefinite access and the free access, I think it's a really great start with the patients that have been affected by it.

"It still doesn't change the fact that it might be removed, and we're still not sure how that will look."

title: What is Garma Festival? Australia's biggest Indigenous gathering returns for 2026
text:
In brief This year's edition of Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering starts on Friday.

Each year, Garma brings together Yolŋu Elders, community leaders, artists, politicians and visitors from across the country.

This article contains references to Indigenous people who have passed.

Thousands of people will travel to north-east Arnhem Land this week as the Garma Festival returns to Yolŋu Country for four days of ceremony, culture and national conversation.

Held on Gumatj Country in the Northern Territory, Garma remains Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering.

This year marks more than a quarter of a century since it started as a small community gathering, and will run from 31 July until 3 August.

Each year it brings together Yolŋu Elders, artists, young people, political leaders, academics, business representatives and visitors from across the country.
