It is a place where ancient ceremony sits alongside some of Australia's biggest conversations about First Nations policy.

This year, those discussions will unfold without Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, despite his commitment last year to attend every Garma while serving as prime minister.

What is Garma Festival?

Hosted by the Yothu Yindi Foundation since 1999, Garma was established to celebrate and strengthen Yolŋu culture while creating a place where Aboriginal knowledge, leadership and ideas could be shared with the broader Australian community.

The word Garma comes from Yolŋu Matha and refers to a meeting place where different ideas come together through a process of two-way learning.

The significance of Gulkula

That philosophy remains central to the festival today. While Garma is grounded in Yolŋu ceremony and tradition, it has also become one of Australia's most influential forums for discussion on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander affairs.

Each year, governments, community organisations, academics and industry leaders travel to Arnhem Land to listen, learn and engage directly with Yolŋu leaders on Country.

Garma is held at Gulkula, a sacred ceremonial site on Gumatj Country near Nhulunbuy in north-east Arnhem Land.

Surrounded by stringybark forest and overlooking the Gulf of Carpentaria, Gulkula has been a place of ceremony and renewal for generations.

According to Yolŋu tradition, it is where the ancestor Ganbulapula introduced the yidaki into Yolŋu life, making it one of the region's most culturally significant places.

Unlike many conferences, Garma is held on Yolŋu Country and led on Yolŋu terms.

Rather than Aboriginal leaders travelling to Canberra, governments, institutions and organisations travel to Arnhem Land, placing First Nations culture, knowledge and authority at the centre of the national conversation.

Visitors camp on Country throughout the four-day festival and are asked to observe cultural protocols guided by their Yolŋu hosts.

Where tradition is shared and strengthened

While Garma has become one of Australia's most influential Indigenous policy forums, culture remains at its heart.

Each day features Buŋgul (ceremonial dance), manikay (song), storytelling and miny'tji (art), shared by Elders and families in the open air. Workshops, youth forums, music performances and exhibitions celebrate the strength and diversity of Aboriginal culture across Arnhem Land and beyond.

Yothu Yindi performed at Garma's 25th anniversary event last year. Source: Supplied / Leicolhn McKellar / Yothu Yindi Foundation

For many visitors, the nightly Buŋgul performances are among the festival's defining moments, as members of the Yolŋu clans perform songlines that have been passed down through countless generations.

The festival is designed not only to preserve Yolŋu cultural practices, but to ensure they continue to be shared with younger generations while inviting visitors to learn through respect, listening and cultural exchange.

From a backyard barbecue to a national institution

This year marks 25 years of Garma.

The festival was envisioned by the late Dr Galarrwuy Yunupiŋu AC and the late Dr M Yunupiŋu as more than a celebration of culture. They saw Garma as a place where Yolŋu authority could shape national conversations, test new ideas and bring Aboriginal and non-Indigenous Australians together through genuine dialogue.

What began as a modest gathering has grown into Australia's largest Indigenous cultural festival.

The festival is designed not only to preserve Yolŋu cultural practices, but to ensure they continue to be shared with younger generations. Source: Supplied / Tiffany Garvie / Yothu Yindi Foundation

Dhapanbal Yunupiŋu, daughter of Dr M Yunupiŋu, has previously recalled the humble beginnings of the first Garma, saying: "There were no tents, two cars, and a BBQ."

Today, thousands of people travel from across Australia to attend the annual gathering.

Why is Garma so politically important?

Over more than two decades, Garma has become one of Australia's most influential Indigenous policy forums.

Politicians, academics, business leaders and Aboriginal organisations have used the festival to discuss issues including land rights, truth-telling, economic development, education, constitutional recognition and the Voice to Parliament.

READ MORE Next-generation Indigenous women are leading the way on employment growth

Many of the conversations that begin at Garma continue well beyond Arnhem Land, influencing national debate and government policy.

Anthony Albanese skips Garma

The prime minister has said he will not attend the 2026 Garma Festival, despite a declaration he made at last year's event that he would return every year he remained prime minister.

"I commit here that every single year that I have the great honour to be Australia's prime minister, I will be here and engaged with you," Albanese said at the time.

Albanese won't attend Garma this year as he'll be on leave at the time. The prime minister has defended the decision, saying he hasn't "[had] a day off all year" and noting that he has attended each year since 2019.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will skip Garma Festival for the first time in years. Source: AAP / Aaron Bunch

The decision has been criticised by some Indigenous leaders, with Northern Land Council chair Matthew Ryan describing the absence as "very disappointing", particularly at a time when Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory face significant challenges.

The Yothu Yindi Foundation acknowledged Albanese had attended every Garma Festival since 2019 and remains a longstanding supporter of the event.

Who is attending Garma in 2026?

Although the prime minister will be absent, senior political and community leaders will still travel to Gulkula for this year's festival.

Among those taking part in keynote addresses and major discussions are National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter, Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy.

They will join Yolŋu Elders, Aboriginal community leaders, and thousands of other visitors from across Australia, reflecting Garma's unique role as both a celebration of living culture and one of the nation's most significant forums on First Nations affairs.

NITV and SBS will have extensive coverage from the Garma Festival beginning Friday 31 July and concluding Monday 3 August. You can watch on SBS and NITV and SBS On Demand.

title: There's something else Neil the seal wrecked in Tasmania — the council's bank account
text:
In brief Neil the seal, the viral southern elephant seal, became the star of Tasmania's Seven Mile Beach.

Managing his antics has left the town's local council with a sizeable repair bill.

Neil the seal captures hearts and global attention during his visits to Tasmania, but his most recent stay racked up a bill of more than $36,000.

The five-year-old elephant seal hauls out twice a year to rest and moult in the island state's south-east, where he was born.

His antics, including crushing bollards and fences, and lounging on quiet beach-side streets, have drawn millions of views on social media.

In June, wildlife authorities issued a blunt public statement, urging people to keep their distance or risk "loving Neil to death".

His 15-day stay at Seven Mile Beach cost the local Clarence City Council a total of $31,540.53 — the majority relating to staffing and labour.

There is also a repair bill for one flattened street sign, 10 knocked-over bollards and one crushed fence, costing council $1,297.70 in materials.

Staff, including a 24-hour security presence, spent 275.5 hours managing traffic and crowds and repairing damage.

Council mayor Brendan Blomeley said the overall bill was relatively small.

Source: AP / Sam Volker

"Neil is a wild animal, and the overexposure and constant public attention he received could have led to a more dramatic outcome," Blomeley said.

"Wherever he decides to come ashore next, I hope he is given the space and time he needs."

Right-to-information documents obtained by the ABC show that Tasmania's natural resources and environment department has spent more than $45,000 managing Neil's four haul-outs in 2025 and 2026.

Neil's June haul-out cost the department $4,794, but it was still calculating the full price tag.

Neil, who currently weighs one tonne, safely returned to sea in early July and is expected to come back to Tasmania later in the year once he's done feeding in the Southern Ocean.

He was rescued by wildlife authorities after being born on a beach in southern Tasmania.

Experts have said his "jousting" with posts and other objects is natural behaviour, and something seals of his age usually do with each other.

There were once southern elephant seals in Tasmania, but they were wiped out by hunting in the early 1800s.

The species is currently listed as vulnerable in Australia.

"Neil is potentially one of the first southern elephant seal pups to be born back in Tasmania," department wildlife expert Kris Carlyon has said.

"Regardless of the resource burden and the challenges that Neil throws, we're pleased to see him."

title: ACMA sues Optus over 2025 network outage and failed Triple Zero calls
text:
In brief Australia's communications watchdog said it will sue Optus over a major 2025 outage.

ACMA alleges Optus made over 1,000 breaches of two legal obligations during the outage.

Australia's second-largest telco is facing legal action over a major network failure that caused a widespread Triple Zero outage.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) alleges Optus breached two legal obligations more than 1,000 times during the outage on 18 September, 2025.

Access to emergency call services was essential to protect the public, the regulator's chair Nerida O'Loughlin said.

"Australians rightly expect that when they call Triple Zero, their call will connect," she said in a statement on Thursday.

"The circumstances of this outage meant that did not reliably occur, leaving people unable to connect to potentially life-saving services.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Giving access to the emergency call service is not optional; it is a fundamental legal obligation, and the most important public safety responsibility telecommunications providers have."

Optus failed to give customers who made Triple Zero calls access to the emergency call service and to ensure those calls were carried appropriately, the regulator alleged.

The proceedings against the Singaporean-owned company announced on Thursday will be heard in the Federal Court.

The maximum penalty is $250,000 per contravention.

Lawsuit follows Optus review, previous $12 million fine

The legal action follows the massive outage which went for almost 14 hours and impacted 600 calls, with 455 failing to connect.

An independent review, released by Optus in December, found there were at least 10 mistakes by the company and its contractor Nokia during an upgrade.

It took Optus and Nokia 13 hours to understand the problem, with an Optus call centre not escalating early concerns from five people who said their Triple Zero calls weren't working, the report by experienced executive Kerry Schott found.

The watchdog has previously taken action against the telco following another Triple Zero outage in November 2023.

The action resulted in Singtel Optus subsidiaries, including Optus Mobile, paying more than $12 million in infringement notice penalties for breaches relating to emergency calls.

"The recurrence of a major network outage affecting emergency calls so soon after the November 2023 outage is a significant concern and one of the reasons the ACMA has decided to take this matter to court," O'Loughlin said.

"The ACMA will not hesitate to take strong enforcement action where alleged telco failures have jeopardised public access to the critical emergency call service."

Optus acknowledged the Federal Court proceedings, adding it would be inappropriate to comment further.

"Our focus remains on building a stronger and better Optus," the company said in a statement to the Australian Associated Press.

READ MORE Three people dead after Optus network upgrade sparked triple-zero call failure

"We continue to invest in network resilience, strengthen our systems and processes, build and foster a culture of transparency and accountability, and improve the services our customers and communities rely on every day.

"This work is being supported by our broader transformation program and implementation of the Dr Schott report recommendations."

The court action comes weeks after Telstra suffered a service outage that left train networks in disarray and customers unable to dial Triple Zero.

title: The $67 million journalism fund claim against Labor — and what the facts show
text:
In brief The Journalism Assistance Fund is a $67.6 million federal government program that subsidises the wages of more than 2,000 journalists at 185 media organisations.

It has sparked debate over independence and editorial influence.

Claims that the federal government is using taxpayer money to bankroll media outlets for favourable coverage have spread online, sparking debate about press independence.

The Journalism Assistance Fund (JAF), launched last November, is a $67.6 million federal government program that subsidises the wages of more than 2,000 journalists at 185 news publishers across Australia.

Critics, including News24 (formerly known as Sky News) commentator Andrew Bolt, say the scheme could influence how outlets cover the government.

But the government says the fund is designed to support public-interest journalism, promote media diversity and help newsrooms navigate ongoing disruption across the media sector.

So what is the JAF, who received the money, and do the criticisms stack up?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is the Journalism Assistance Fund?

The JAF is a key part of the federal government's broader News Media Assistance Program, announced in 2024 and designed to support public-interest journalism and media diversity.

It provides grants to eligible Australian organisations that publish digital "core news content" that reports, investigates or explains issues relevant to informing democratic decision-making or current events of public significance.

Lifestyle, entertainment, celebrity, real estate and sponsored content are excluded, as are opinion and editorial pieces.

The grants subsidise part of the cost of employing full-time journalists, providing up to $13,000 per journalist each year, or $39,000 over the three-year life of the program.

According to the funding guidelines, the program aims to support Australian news publishers and the continued employment of journalists producing public-interest journalism.

The government says the scheme was in response to years of financial pressure on the news industry, as publishers face declining advertising revenue, newsroom closures and increasing competition from digital platforms such as Alphabet and Meta.

In a speech last week, Communications Minister Anika Wells said the fund was about sustaining public-interest journalism across Australia and rejected suggestions it could influence editorial decisions.

Communications Minister Anika Wells rejected suggestions the fund would influence editorial decisions. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

"This support is not conditional on what stories are written, and anything to the contrary is an insult to Australian journalists. Our media sector is strong and mature and I know they do and will continue to hold people to account, including those in government," she said.

The funding guidelines do not require outlets to acknowledge receipt of program funding, but state that, if an acknowledgement is included, it should state that the funding "does not influence the production of specific content".

Only Australian-owned or controlled news organisations meeting the eligibility criteria could apply.

Applications were assessed on a first-come, first-served basis, with the program closing less than a month after the available funding was exhausted.

In total, 185 Australian news publishers received funding, including 93 regional publishers, 23 culturally and linguistically diverse publishers, 22 suburban publishers and two First Nations publishers.

Who received the funding?

The largest grants went to Australia's major commercial media companies.

Nine was the largest beneficiary, receiving $16.1 million across two grants.

The largest individual grant ($8.16 million) went to Fairfax Media Limited, which publishes The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and The Australian Financial Review. Nine acquired Fairfax in 2018, but the grant was listed under Fairfax Media Limited.

Nine Entertainment, which includes the company's television network, received a further $7.96 million.

Seven West Media was given a total of $11.33 million, with its television network receiving $5.6 million.

However, many independent and regional publishers also received funding.

SA Today, which owns regional South Australian newspapers, received $2.7 million.

Regional Publishers, which owns The Courier in Ballarat, received $2.28 million. The Conversation received $1.03 million, while dozens of smaller regional and community news organisations also received grants.

Foreign-owned publishers, including News Corp and The Guardian Australia, were ineligible under the scheme. The ABC and SBS were also excluded because they already receive public funding.

The full list of organisations that received funding, along with the amounts, is publicly available on GrantConnect.

Why has the fund become controversial?

One News Nation, which describes itself as an independent "centre-right" news outlet, appeared to be the first to report the full list of recipients last week.

According to an ABC News Verify investigation, the outlet publishes pro-One Nation content and its social media page recently rebranded from the "One Nation Supporters Network", though it denies it is affiliated with the party.

In social media posts, the outlet accused the government of "quietly paying journalist wages" and claimed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was deciding "who counts as news".

READ MORE How to check your offset account is working properly after $55 million error exposed

The posts received thousands of likes, with many comments accusing the government of "bribing" the media for favourable coverage.

Bolt also criticised the program, saying funded organisations should disclose the government support.

"I'm not saying all these journalists toe the Labor line as a result of the money, but shouldn't they at least declare this government money at the bottom of every one of their articles?" he asked.

He added: "I think it's a corrupting influence because it makes journalists and media outlets look to the government and not want to offend the government."

In a separate News24 segment, Rita Panahi claimed the funds were mostly flowing to left-wing media outlets.

Does government funding influence journalism?

Media experts say the central question is whether funding journalism is different from funding editorial content.

Joanne Gray, chair of discipline, media and communications at the University of Sydney, said she thought it was unlikely the recipients were coming under political influence of the government, and there has been no evidence that recipients have altered their editorial coverage because of the grants.

"Governments often fund news and journalism through various models, and it's common throughout the world, and it's common in Australia," she told SBS News.

"As long as the funds are transparent and people are adhering to journalistic standards, and they're reviewing it, I don't see funds having or causing a problem of bias or being politicised or being misused for political reasons."

Matthew Ricketson, a communications professor at Deakin University, said he believed criticisms that the funds could influence editorial content were a "half-truth".

"If government is funding the media, there are certainly things to look out for and be wary of," he said.

But he said publicly funded broadcasters such as the ABC and SBS had maintained their independence.

"I'd add that newspapers, whether online or historically in print, have received government advertising for well over 100 years," he told SBS News.

"Nobody seriously has argued that has unduly influenced those newspapers to write positive things about governments when they didn't want to."

A spokesperson from the Department of Communications said the federal government believed "a strong, sustainable and diverse news sector is a critical element of a healthy democracy — supporting an informed citizenry and social cohesion".

"As part of the News Media Assistance Program, the Journalism Assistance Fund supports news organisations to keep journalists employed and produce public interest news that informs Australians," the spokesperson said.

"As with all Government grant processes, funding was awarded following assessment against eligibility criteria stated in the Grant Guidelines available at business.gov.au.

"The grant was open to all Australian-based news organisations that produce core news content that is digitally distributed."

title: Treasurer welcomes 'encouraging' numbers as inflation falls to pre-war level
text:
In brief Housing remained the biggest contributor to inflation in the June figures.

The Reserve Bank is due to meet on 10 and 11 August to make its next interest rate decision.

An unexpected drop in Australia's inflation has eased fears of another imminent interest rate hike.

The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data showed headline inflation — the total inflation rate in an economy, including volatile items like fuel — falling from 4 per cent to 3.8 per cent in June.

It's now at its lowest level since 28 February, when the US and Israel launched an attack on Iran.

Trimmed mean inflation — which measures underlying inflation without volatile items and is the preferred measure by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) — remained steady at 3.6 per cent, defying central bank predictions of a rise to 3.8 per cent.

The fall in inflation coincided with transport costs moderating for the month, ABS head of price statistics Rachel McCrick said.

"Lower world oil prices as a result of some stabilisation in the Middle East in June contributed to fuel prices falling 10.9 per cent in the month," she said on Wednesday.

"The federal government's fuel excise relief measures, which contributed to lower automatic fuel prices in April and May, also remained in place."

The fuel excise measures reduced the cost of fuel by 32 cents a litre during the month.

However, the measure was reduced to just 16 cents in July, and will be phased out entirely from Sunday.

Source: SBS News

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the inflation figures were reassuring following a period of economic volatility.

"It's an encouraging outcome that shows we've made progress on inflation since the budget, even in the face of intense global uncertainty," he said.

"Treasury has warned that the next phase of the conflict could be more challenging for the global economy, with the oil market now more vulnerable."

Quarterly inflation numbers showed headline inflation falling from 4 to 3.9 per cent.

Meanwhile, the trimmed mean rose from 3.5 per cent in the March quarter to 3.6 per cent in the June quarter.

READ MORE Drivers warned about key dates as government confirms fuel discount's end

Housing remained the biggest contributor to inflation in the June monthly figures, rising by 6.8 per cent.

"Annual inflation for new dwellings has reached its highest level in almost three years, at 5.8 per cent," McCrick said.

"This was driven by builders passing on higher material and labour costs."

How will new inflation numbers impact interest rates?

The head of economic research at Oxford Economics Australia, Harry Murphy Cruise, said the RBA would be focused less on the headline figures and more on the breadth of price rises.

"Underlying inflation is not just resisting pressure to rise. In quarterly terms, it is continuing to ease," he said.

"All that backs up our view that the RBA will keep rates on hold next month."

The RBA is due to meet on 10 and 11 August to decide whether interest rates will rise from current levels of 4.35 per cent, or keep them on hold.

READ MORE Albanese flags new fuel announcements as petrol prices tipped to spike further

The bank's governor, Michele Bullock, said on Tuesday that higher interest rates were slowing the economy as expected.

The past four years of above-target inflation had been a cautionary tale for the Reserve Bank board, she said.

"The longer it is out of target, the more concerned that the board becomes," Bullock told a fundraising lunch at the Anika Foundation in Sydney.

"It is quite at the front of their minds. In the May forecast we had it coming back under 3 [per cent] towards the end of 2027, and that's a long time to be above target."

title: Drivers warned about key dates as government confirms fuel discount's end
text:
In Brief Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed the fuel excise discount will end on 2 August.

Drivers can expect prices to rise by a "few cents per litre" starting Monday.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed the fuel excise discount will end on Sunday 2 August, ending weeks of uncertainty over whether the discount would be extended for a second time.

"It was never the government's intention for [the discount] to be permanent," Chalmers said on Wednesday.

The initial discount of 32c per litre ended in June, after which the government extended the fuel excise cut at a reduced rate of 16c per litre.

"We began to taper that off at the start of the month, deliberately, so that we could provide a bit more cost of living help," Chalmers said.

While the NRMA does expect a modest rise in petrol prices from Monday, the roadside assistance and travel organisation doesn't expect costs to skyrocket.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Our message to the public is: We know fuel prices are going to go up on Monday and beyond. We don't know by how much," NRMA spokesperson Peter Khoury told SBS News.

"We would expect average prices to go up a few cents per litre ... but it really depends on the service station."

Companies showing 'restraint'

The announcement ended weeks of uncertainty over whether the government would extend the fuel excise discount after Iran resumed its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, sending global oil markets into shock for the second time since the US-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic in February.

Khoury said global oil markets were already responding to news on Monday that both sides had halted bombing, with benchmark unleaded prices dropping.

If the relative calm continues, Khoury said it will "definitely negate the increases we're going to get from the tax being reintroduced".

"We've seen a lot of restraint from the oil companies in the past few weeks," he said, adding that if global oil prices continued to fall it would "cushion the blow" of upcoming price rises in Australia.

By how much will prices go up?

Khoury said that price rises caused by the end of the fuel excise discount wouldn't happen overnight.

"It will be gradual, it won't be immediate," he said.

"Not every service station is going to put their price up by 17 cents a litre. In fact, almost none will. So please don't go out and panic buy."

Khoury told SBS News that, by the time the discount expires, it's likely the increase will be closer to 17 cents rather than the extended excise reduction rate of 16 cents.

"We think it's going to be another cent because of the inflation adjustment, which also just happens to land on the same day [Monday] they do that twice a year."

Just how much cost will be passed on to the consumer depends on individual service stations, Khoury added.

"We don't want people to panic because some service stations will go up on Monday and others won't; it really depends on when they sell their stock."

In any case, the fuel excise discount is being wound up against the backdrop of retail prices that are already steadily rising.

"The national average for unleaded is about $1.93, and we're expecting that to continue to increase based on the increases we've seen for wholesale prices," Khoury said.

That's a 13-cent increase from the $1.80 per litre calculated by the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission as the average petrol price in major cities on 22 July.

As of 21 July, Australia has 42 days of fuel reserves, with an expected 3.1 billion litres of crude, diesel, jet fuel, and petrol scheduled to arrive over the next four weeks, according to the federal government.

title: Could Qantas' record-breaking new plane make stopovers a thing of the past?
text:
In brief A record-breaking Qantas flight has flown for more than 24 hours as part of the airline's bid to offer nonstop flights to London.

But experts say the ultra-long-haul flight isn't necessarily a replacement for flights with stopovers.

A record-breaking test flight lasting more than 24 hours has touched down in France from Melbourne — and experts say Australia could be leading the world on the new technology use.

Qantas' specially adapted Airbus A350-1000ULR landed in France on Tuesday after a marathon 24 hours and 24 minutes in the air, covering 23,057km without stopping — the longest direct flight ever attempted by a commercial aircraft.

The flight is part of a two-month test campaign as part of Qantas' Project Sunrise, which aims to launch the world's longest commercial passenger flight and reshape long-haul travel by offering direct flights from Australia's east coast to London and New York.

The previous record belonged to a Boeing 777-200LR, which flew 21,601.7km from Hong Kong to London in 22 hours and 42 minutes back in 2005.

Qantas has ordered 12 of the modified A350 aircraft, each fitted with an extra 20,000-litre fuel tank and configured to seat 238 passengers.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The first is due for delivery in April 2027, with daily non-stop flights between Sydney and London planned from October that year — turning what was once a five-day journey in 1947 on the old 'Kangaroo Route' into a single hop of 19 to 21 hours, depending on winds and routing.

The airline has said a Sydney-New York route will follow shortly after the launch of the London route.

Could stopovers become a thing of the past?

The test flight's success has cast eyes towards the future of air travel, with some wondering whether stopovers in Singapore, Dubai or Los Angeles may be a thing of the past.

But that's not quite where we're headed, experts say.

Justin Brownjohn from RMIT University's Aviation Academy says non-stop routes will keep becoming more viable as aircraft range improves and fuel use falls — but that doesn't make them a replacement for one-stop flying.

"Airlines have historically competed on network and frequency, but Project Sunrise competes on time," he said.

READ MORE Where Australian luxury travellers are heading in 2026 — and what it could cost

"Cutting up to four hours off the journey from Sydney to London and removing the connection entirely is a different product, not an improved version of the existing one.

"These services won't replace one-stop flying, they'll sit alongside it."

Brownjohn expects the strongest demand for the ultra-long-haul services to come from business and premium leisure travellers willing to pay more for the time saved — and says the wider effect may be felt most by the Middle Eastern and Asian hub airports that have built their business models around the layover.

'A different physiological event'

Spending over 20 hours in the air also raises real questions about passenger wellbeing.

"Twenty hours is not a longer flight, it is a different physiological event," Brownjohn said. "On this flight comfort has stopped being a luxury feature and become the thing being sold."

Peter Cistulli, professor of sleep medicine at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, worked with Qantas on the physiological side of the aircraft's design.

Qantas' Project Sunrise envisions nonstop long-haul flights. Source: AAP / James Ross

"Project Sunrise takes ultra-long-haul flights to a whole new level," Cistulli told SBS News.

"It's arguably the final frontier of travel on Earth, so it brings a whole lot of additional challenges, including the biological challenge of crossing so many time zones over a short period and how that can influence your health and wellbeing."

Cistulli, who also worked with the airline on its long-haul Dreamliner aircraft, said compressing so many time zones into one flight leaves the body's circadian system less time to adjust.

He says researchers' input on elements including lighting, meal timing, and in-flight exercise is intended to help passengers adapt to their destination time zone faster.

The aircraft has what Qantas describes as the lowest seat density of any comparable jet, with more than 40 per cent of the 238 seats allocated to premium cabins.

A wellness zone will also offer stretch handles, refreshments, and a guided, video-led movement program.

But Cistulli is also candid about the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), with long periods of immobility already proven to raise DVT risk.

While he says the baseline risk on any flight is already low at under 1 per cent, those with "heightened risk" of DVT may not be suitable for the ultra-long-haul flight.

For the average person, however, concerns about the lengthy flight can be mitigated by adequate physical activity on board.

He says that opting for stopovers has both its pros and cons when it comes to health. Being able to get off a flight and move around in an airport is a benefit, he says, but that also adds to the journey and can increase fatigue.

"Of course, not everybody would choose to be cooped up in a plane for 20-plus hours — the stopover options will always remain there. Passengers will have their choice."

Australia's shrinking distance problem

Cistulli sees Project Sunrise as part of Australia's long fight against the "tyranny of distance" it's grappled with as a geographically isolated nation.

"This is the ultimate frontier, in that we're bringing the world closer to Australia and Australia closer to the world," he says. "It's a really fantastic story for Australia, and it's no surprise that an Australian airline would go to the trouble of solving this problem."

READ MORE A travel charge most Australians don't know they pay is rising again

Whether Qantas holds onto the bragging rights is another question.

Singapore Airlines already operates the world's longest scheduled commercial route — a roughly 19-hour service between Singapore and New York.

"I think it will be interesting to see what the competition do," he says. "This will definitely give Qantas a competitive advantage, but whether that's long-lived, time will tell."

The extended range also opens up more than just one route. With planes capable of covering these distances, almost any city pairing becomes commercially viable if there's demand for it.

READ MORE 'Unpredictable': New warning for Australians travelling abroad

It also gives Qantas more flexibility to route around trouble spots, including current airspace restrictions due to the war in the Middle East, opening up options such as flying to London over the North Pole instead.

Cistulli is careful to frame Project Sunrise as an addition to the market, not a replacement for it.

"I think it's all about choice, and tailoring the opportunity for particular customer needs," he said. "This just adds a new option for people who do need to get somewhere in a hurry, so to speak — and I think that's a great addition."

title: How to check your offset account is working properly after $55 million error exposed
text:
IN BRIEF A review by ASIC found banks paid over $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

Experts said Australians should check whether their offset account has been set up and managed correctly.

Australians have lost millions of dollars to offset account errors, according to a review by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC).

The corporate regulator analysed the offset practices of eight banks, which it said represent more than 70 per cent of Australia's $2.5 trillion home loan market.

It found weaknesses in how all banks established, monitored and managed offset accounts.

Reports to ASIC between September 2023 and August 2025 showed that banks paid over $55 million in customer compensation for offset account failures.

In some cases, customers were repaid over $17,000 due to system limitations or administrative errors.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What exactly is an offset account?

Offset accounts operate like everyday transaction accounts, which can be used to deposit and withdraw money. But they're often marketed as a simple way to reduce home loan interest.

That's because money held in an offset account also reduces the outstanding amount owed on a home loan, which is used to calculate the interest paid on that loan.

If a person has $50,000 in their offset account and a $750,000 loan, they will only be charged interest on $700,000.

Source: SBS News

Sally Tindall, director of data insights at Canstar, said offset accounts are a popular choice for many Australian mortgage holders.

"For many customers, it's one of the most powerful tools borrowers have to reduce the amount of interest they pay on their mortgage — but only if it's working as intended."

However, offset accounts are often associated with higher interest rates, additional account fees or a combination of both.

Check your offset account is linked

ASIC encouraged Australians to check whether their offset account was actually set up following their initial request.

Information about offset accounts should be available via a bank's mobile app, online banking or bank statements.

Some bank sites have mortgage offset pages which outline whether a person is eligible for an offset and how to find their account number.

ASIC's report also warned that refinancing or switching home loan products could break the link between an offset account and a person's mortgage.

In just over a month, a customer paid more than $3,500 in additional interest because their offset account was not linked, ASIC found.

Tindall said: "When you've spent years building up savings in your offset, the last thing you want is for those dollars to be sitting in an account that's not actually reducing your interest bill."

"But don't stop there, do some quick maths to make sure the interest you're being charged is on the amount you actually owe, factoring in the offset balance."

What to do if something looks wrong

Customers with complaints or questions should contact their bank directly.

According to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), if a person formally raises a complaint with their bank, they must respond within 21 days for complaints involving financial difficulty or 30 days for other issues.

If a person is not satisfied with their result, they can escalate the matter to AFCA, which will act as an independent mediator at no charge.

Under the Code of Banking Practice, banks have procedures in place to deal with and resolve complaints. Source: AAP

Kathy Tannous, an economics professor at Western Sydney University, told SBS News customers can take small steps to improve their financial literacy and understanding about their offset account.

She said people should "constantly review" their home loan statements and loan repayment schedules.

"I know these days it is a lot harder because there are many branches that are closed. It's also much harder to talk to an individual because we've got lovely chatbots and so on.

"But I would say, be persistent, because the time that you're spending on this may actually save you quite a bit of money."

title: The new plan to prevent data centres from driving power prices up
text:
In brief A new plan would force data centres to invest in renewable energy.

There are fears the power-hungry data centres could cause price hikes for electricity.

Large-scale data centres will be forced to invest in additional renewable energy to fuel their operations and avoid causing power price hikes in regulations agreed to by all but two states and territories.

The Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council revealed its plans late on Tuesday after meeting to discuss advice on the issue from the Australian Energy Market Commission.

Climate groups welcomed the announcement and boost for renewable energy, but an organisation representing data centre operators warned the policy could be counterproductive if designed without their input.

The changes come weeks after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced plans to require data centres to be powered by clean energy projects under a shake-up of artificial intelligence rules, and after a NSW data centre inquiry heard similar calls for action.

The council, which includes energy ministers from the federal government and all state and territory governments, met virtually to discuss data centre energy proposals after flagging the issue in May.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

All ministers except those from Queensland and the Northern Territory agreed to pursue regulations that would "mandate that data centres offset their electricity demand by investing in additional renewable generation", the meeting communique said.

Renewable energy would need to be generated near the data centre unless local authorities opted out of the requirement, and the rules would be set at a national level, although states and territories could add additional requirements.

Changes to national rules would be considered in September, including reforms to the way data centres reported energy use.

The Climate Council called the proposed changes encouraging, although chief executive Amanda McKenzie said the rules should give data centre operators strict deadlines.

Governments from all Australian states and territories should also support the changes, she said, to avoid penalising some consumers with rising power bills.

"Unless these hold-out governments get on board, Queenslanders and Territorians will be left paying higher power bills, and we will all pay the price of higher climate pollution," she said.

But introducing a blanket rule for data centres' energy use could be ineffective if it was not designed with industry input, Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett said.

Each centre operated differently to meet customer demands and use renewable energy, she told attendees at the Australian Clean Energy Summit, and removing options could produce poor results or deter investments.

"A one-size-fits-all approach will not work and may well be counterproductive to renewable energy investment objectives," Dennett said.

"The risk of removing this flexibility and taking a one-size-fits-all approach to energy procurement and offset arrangements may have consequences for how the data centre sector approaches renewable energy, and it's why good policy design matters and why industry needs to be at the table."

Amplia Therapeutics has received encouraging lab results which highlighted the use of its lead drug narmafotinib, saying it can attack several of the nastier features that make the cancer so hard to treat. The research, led by Professor Paul Timpson and colleagues at Sydney’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research, was the results of extensive laboratory work on narmafotinib in pancreatic cancer models and was posted online on the biology preprint server bioRxiv. Amplia Therapeutics’ says fresh preclinical research data has strengthened the case for its drug candidate narmafotinib against pancreatic cancer cells, pictured. Amplia says the work adds further evidence that narmafotinib, a focal adhesion kinase (FAK) inhibitor, may improve outcomes by targeting tumour fibrosis, chemotherapy resistance and metastatic spread - three big hurdles in a disease that remains one of cancer medicine’s toughest assignments. FAK is a protein inside cells that acts like a control switch for movement, survival and attachment. It sits where cells anchor to their surrounding environment and helps tell them whether to grow, move or shut themselves down.

Advertisement

‘The research conducted by Professor Timpson’s team over recent years is now being shared with the broader scientific community.’ Amplia Therapeutics chief executive office and managing director Dr Chris Burns In many cancers, FAK becomes overactive or over-produced, helping tumour cells survive, move and spread. That has made it a target for cancer-fighting drugs such as narmafotinib. Among the key findings, the paper reported reduced tumour fibrosis and enhanced anti-tumour activity when narmafotinib was combined with chemotherapy. Other results included reduced cancer dissemination and metastatic spread in a pancreatic cancer model and the down-regulation – or diminished activity - of multiple genes linked to chemotherapy resistance. In this case, the drug appears to turn down genes that usually help cancer cells resist chemotherapy. The effect is to weaken the cancer cells’ defences, leaving chemotherapy better able to do its job and potentially lowering the number of cancer cells that remain alive after treatment. Amplia Therapeutics chief executive officer and managing director Dr Chris Burns said: “These studies strengthen the scientific rationale for the clinical development of narmafotinib and provide further insight into the multifaceted mechanisms through which narmafotinib can act in the treatment of this devastating disease.”

Advertisement

The update follows a busy clinical run for the Melbourne-based biotech. In May, Amplia launched the first stage of a Phase 2b registration-enabling pancreatic cancer study that will test daily dosing of narmafotinib with the chemotherapy drugs gemcitabine and Abraxane in newly diagnosed advanced pancreatic cancer patients. A registration-enabling study is a pivotal clinical trial designed to produce the core evidence needed to support an application for approval to market a new drug. Its job is to show that a treatment is safe at the proposed dose, that it helps patients and that the data package is strong enough for regulators such as the US Food and Drug Administration or Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration to assess. The study is expected to enrol 12 patients across two dose cohorts at three or four Australian sites, with patient enrolment planned for the fourth quarter of this year. Amplia’s June quarterly also underlined why the company is pressing ahead. Mature ACCENT trial data presented at the American Association for Cancer Research showed favourable safety and encouraging efficacy for narmafotinib, with a 36 per cent overall response rate and a 70 per cent disease control rate, compared with 50 per cent for chemotherapy alone. The data also showed median overall survival of 11.1 months — an improvement of more than two months — and progression-free survival of 7.7 months when narmafotinib was used with standard chemotherapy.

Advertisement

The company ended the June quarter with $24 million in cash, giving it a handy buffer as it pushes narmafotinib further into pancreatic cancer and prepares to test the same drug in a second oncology target. That expansion comes through PRROSE, a phase two trial being run under an agreement with the Australia New Zealand Gynaecological Oncology Group (ANZGOG) to evaluate narmafotinib alongside standard chemotherapy in 15 to 20 patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer. For Amplia, the latest paper is not a clinical result — but it is another useful building block. And in a field where every extra piece of biological support counts, the company will no doubt be happy to bank more evidence as it heads toward the next stage of its pancreatic cancer program. Anthropic has revealed its Claude artificial intelligence models broke into the computer systems of three real companies during safety testing, days after rival OpenAI disclosed a similar failure. The models were told they were working inside a sealed practice environment with no connection to the internet, but a set-up error meant they were not. When Claude went hunting for a way into its practice target and found real companies instead, it treated them as part of the game and broke in. On June 13, Anthropic suspended worldwide access to its two most powerful AI models. Bloomberg It did not need anything sophisticated. Anthropic said the models got in through weak passwords and systems left open without a login. The company found three incidents after reviewing 141,006 test runs, a check it began after OpenAI said on July 21 that several of its models had broken out of a locked-down test and reached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face. Unable to reach the fake target, the model went after the real one and got hold of passwords and a database holding several hundred records of real business data. Anthropic called it the most serious of the three, and the only one where a model kept going after working out the target was real. In the second, Claude found a note inside the practice environment telling staff to download a piece of software that did not exist. So it wrote its own booby-trapped version, set up an email address and an account, and uploaded it to a public library used by programmers worldwide. It sat there for about an hour and was downloaded onto 15 real computers. One belonged to a security firm that automatically installs new software to check it for viruses, which let Claude’s code steal that firm’s passwords and reach further into its systems. The model’s own written reasoning shows it saw the danger. If this were the real internet, it noted, publishing the software would be “NOT okay, and surely not the intended solution”. It then talked itself into believing the whole thing was staged and so carried on.

Advertisement

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. Bloomberg A third model, an experimental version never released to the public, scanned about 9000 possible targets and broke into one company’s website before it realised the system was real and stopped. Related Article Exclusive

AI ChatGPT’s evil twin: How criminals and extremists are using AI to lay traps Anthropic said none of the models tried to escape or chase goals of its own, and that the protections built into the versions of Claude that the public uses would have blocked all of it. The company was contacted for further comment. It has stopped running hacking tests that can reach the internet. Ian Rogers, a former Apple executive now working on AI security at digital security company Ledger, said the incident was a preview. “This happened in one of the world’s best-resourced AI labs,” he said. “Soon, there will be millions of AI agents connected to our email, calendars, financial accounts and enterprise systems.”

Advertisement

The three companies were told on July 27, and two had no idea they had been hacked. Irregular said its investigation was continuing and that it appreciated Anthropic’s “collaboration and transparency”. Related Article AI Silicon Valley’s AI spending spree comes with an Australian invoice Liming Zhu, a CSIRO research director working with the Australian AI Safety Institute on the problem, said the setup error explained most of what happened but not all of it. A well-behaved system should turn cautious when the evidence stops matching its instructions, he said, and the model that kept going after working out the target was real showed poor judgement under pressure. He was warier about treating the newest model’s decision to stop as progress, calling it “an encouraging observation, not an established trend”. It had still scanned thousands of systems and broken into one before it pulled up. The bigger issue for Australian businesses, Zhu said, is that ordinary AI assistants sold for everyday work keep the same hacking abilities under the bonnet. A badly worded instruction or too much system access can bring them out.

Advertisement

Pre-release safety testing is the main check on what frontier models can do before they reach the public, and governments, including Australia’s, are weighing how far to rely on that self-testing. After the OpenAI breach, the Australian Signals Directorate issued a public warning saying that the case showed what powerful AI systems will soon be capable of, and the new Australian AI Safety Institute briefed federal departments. Neither body can compel an AI company to report anything, however. The federal government dropped its plan for mandatory rules covering high-risk AI, and while the European Union and California already require serious AI incidents to be disclosed, Australia does not. title: ‘Pretty surreal’: Accidental star of La La Land concert to play in Los Angeles this weekend
text:
Advertisement

CultureMoviesLive music ‘Pretty surreal’: Accidental star of La La Land concert to play in Los Angeles this weekend Garry Maddox July 31, 2026 — 12:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two months ago, Sterling Nasa was sitting in the Sydney audience of La La Land In Concert when Oscar-winning composer-conductor Justin Hurwitz came out after interval to ask if there was an amazing keyboard player in the audience who could take over for a sick musician. The 21-year-old university student, encouraged by his friend Scarlett, stepped up and became the accidental star of the show. “I’ve really got only one shot to give it my best”: Sterling Nasa at the piano. George Chan An incident that sounded like it could have come from the script of La La Land, the musical romance between a jazz musician (played by Ryan Gosling) and an aspiring actress (Emma Stone), went viral around the world. An article in this masthead was followed up by, among many media outlets, The New York Times, The Washington Post, the BBC, The Guardian and CNN. Now Nasa has taken up an invitation by Hurwitz to play piano at La La Land In Concert in Los Angeles – the real La La Land – on Saturday night (Sunday AEST).

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Film A musician was too sick to play, so the call went out to the audience. Sterling ran to the stage He will perform at the famous Greek Theatre in Griffith Park, near the landmark observatory that features in the film. “It’s pretty surreal,” Nasa said from his hotel room in Los Angeles. “You’d never think that just going to a concert at [ICC Sydney Theatre] Darling Harbour on Saturday night would lead to getting an opportunity like this. I’m incredibly grateful and I’m stoked.” Nasa, who has been joined by Scarlett on the trip, said he initially thought Hurwitz’s offer “to do a show” meant joining one of the final performances on the Australian tour. “I got on a call with him and he explained that, no, it was a show at the Greek Theatre in LA,” he said. “It’s the 10th anniversary concert and I’m playing the principal piano part.”

Advertisement

In Sydney, Nasa had to play celeste, also known as a bell-piano, for the first time within 90 seconds of arriving on stage. Nervous for the first 10 minutes, he settled to the point of improvising the difficult-to-sight-read synth solo in the John Legend song Start a Fire. He started a fire of his own. Loading “People who I know from places like Nova Scotia, Boston, parts of Scotland were contacting me saying, “Oh, you were in our local newspaper’,” he said. While he has been practising consistently ahead of the Los Angeles concert, Nasa expects to be nervous again.

Advertisement

“It’s a different book from the one I played the other time,” he said. “It’s the piano book, which is a lot harder. I guess there’s some level of expectation this time. “As fun as [Sydney was] – and it was an amazing experience and you wouldn’t change anything – the crowd and the general vibe of the evening really wanted it to work. Now I want to make sure it’s a good performance.” Nasa, who had just finished his final week studying international relations at uni before the Sydney concert, said the accidental performance had made him wonder if he might have a career as a pianist. As well as playing piano at his local church on Sunday mornings, he plays organ and teaches bagpipes at his old school, Scots College. “I’ve certainly seen that there are legitimate opportunities out there,” he said. “I’ve definitely gotten to understand the industry a lot more.” Part of that has been observing Hurwitz behind the scenes.

Advertisement

Backstage selfie after the Sydney concert: Sterling Nasa (right) with Justin Hurwitz. Stirling Nasa “Obviously being a part of it from the get-go and not just from the end of intermission … it shows you how these things work,” he said. “He’s someone who’s very much at the top at the top of his game, and I’d say top of the game as far as Hollywood composers go. “So it’s cool to get to be involved in that [and] very valuable knowledge for someone of my age.” Nasa recognises that, however surreal going from half a show in Darling Harbour to the main piano part in LA seems, he has to play as well as he can for one performance. “I’ve really got only one shot to give it my best,” he said. “I’m the kind of person who just really wants to leave it all out there. So I want to just make sure it’s a good run.”

Advertisement

His hope is that it will be a great experience. “I’m just in it for what I can learn from it,” he said. “If there are to be other opportunities that come from this, I’d be incredibly grateful. [But] it’s a really beautiful thing to come out of what was a very random, coincidental, lovely night that happened in Sydney.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox. title: ‘Tricky, not dishonest’: ICAC witness dodges questions about fake invoices
text:
Advertisement

Follow our live coverage of the ICAC hearing here. NSW Liberal apparatchik and Reformers member Robert Assaf has told a corruption inquiry that fake invoices sent for work that was never carried out were part of a “tricky” tax scheme rather than dishonesty. Assaf, who formed the right-wing Catholic group within the Liberals, on Friday told the Independent Commission Against Corruption that he knew of the “concept” of illegal donations but never thought the Reformers were doing anything wrong in accepting payments, including from hotelier Michael O’Hara. NSW Reformers founder Robert Assaf arrives at ICAC on Friday. James Brickwood The ICAC is probing whether undeclared political donations were made by prohibited donors, including O’Hara, to a company called Beckington. The donations were intended to support the Reformers.

Advertisement

Assaf said he was aware of the “concept” of prohibited donors and knew that some donations to political parties needed to be declared over a threshold, but did not think the Reformers were doing anything wrong. “If someone told me [at] any point before I got my first summons to this, that what I had done was a problem, I would have gone straight to the electoral commission and reported it and sorted it out,” Assaf said. “I can’t recall any time where we discussed ‘are we doing something wrong?’; we never thought that way.” Assaf has told the commission on Friday that O’Hara paid Beckington, rather than the Reformers directly, for “tricky” tax purposes rather than to hide potentially unlawful political donations.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny They claim they didn’t know the rules. So why go to such absurd lengths to hide the cash? Commissioner Fabian Gleeson asked Assaf a “straightforward honesty question”. “I’m asking you to put aside for the moment the question of whether or not it’s appropriate from a tax perspective, do you think it’s honest at the time?” Gleeson asked. “Did you think it was honest for Beckington to issue an invoice claiming money for consultancy services that it said it was providing Mr O’Hara’s company, when in fact no such consultancy services were being provided, as we understand the evidence?” Assaf said he would have thought it was “tricky”.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Analysis

Operation Rosny The self-styled Braveheart crusader now accused of branch stacking “Why do you have a difficulty, Mr Assaf, in distinguishing between tricky and honest conduct?” Gleeson asked. “Why do you characterise them as merely tricky, but you seem to baulk at the characterisation that it’s dishonest conduct by Beckington?” Assaf said he was not aware of how problematic it was, and just thought of it as tricky in an accounting sense. Assaf told the commission that he and other Reformers were “immature and young” and used money from the group as an advance for personal expenditure, which he says they would pay back. In one case, Reformers cash was used to pay for a buck’s party – either for Assaf or Christian Ellis, although he could not remember which since both men got married about the same time.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Operation Rosny Jean-Claude Perrottet deserved payment for branch stacking, ICAC hears Senior right-wing MP Damien Tudehope, who has featured heavily in evidence this week through his role in backing the religious group the Reformers, will appear before the commission on Monday. Tudehope has stood aside from Liberal leader Kellie Sloane’s frontbench while the inquiry is under way because of his ties to many of the witnesses. He has denied any wrongdoing and is not a person of interest. On Tuesday, a businessman called Frits Mare will appear. Mare gave explosive evidence to the 2023 parliamentary inquiry into branch stacking in The Hills Shire Council. That inquiry heard Jean-Claude Perrottet and Christian Ellis, both persons of interest in this ICAC inquiry, asked Mare for $50,000 to fund a branch operation to unseat Scott Morrison’s right-hand man Alex Hawke from his federal electorate. Mare wanted no part in their scheme.

Advertisement

The bulk of the week will then be spent hearing from Perrottet, who was a key member of the Reformers. The inquiry heard this week that Perrottet paid for branch memberships and also wanted to be paid for his work stacking branches.
