title: ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Wow’ moments, dominators and draft bolters: We rank the top 30 AFL draft prospects Marc McGowan July 31, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to our first top 30 for this year’s AFL draft class. This is not a mock draft, but rather a ranking of prospects based on performance, potential, injury risk and intangibles, based on discussions with recruiting staff at 10 AFL clubs, junior coaches, and this masthead’s own views. As always, there were players who narrowly missed out, such as Benji van Rooyen, Marlon Neocleous, Koby LeCras, Brady Wright, Albert Macgowan, Jordan Knapp, Anthony Long, Harvey Spawton-Guy, Harvie Cooke and Will Antrobus. The likes of Sebastian Marsic and Sydney Swans academy products Aidan McCartney (also North Melbourne father-son eligible), Mason McGroder – a highly promising long jumper – and Jake Medved are also on clubs’ radar. 1.

Advertisement

Cochrane is yet to play this year because of a knee injury, but will make his return on Sunday for Port Adelaide’s SANFL team, alongside his AFL-listed brother Tom. The AFL approved the Power’s request in November for the super prospect – who can just about play anywhere on the ground – to be draft eligible as part of their Next Generation Academy. Cochrane’s been regarded as the top prospect in the 2026 draft class since he dominated the under-16s championships. He is a great athlete, marks the ball well, is an excellent kick, makes smart decisions and should end up as a goalkicking midfielder and genuine difference-maker. 2. Butler could be the first player picked who is not tied to an AFL club – and might be the most talented prospect in the pool. His kicking skills are peerless, including executing kicks that others cannot, and his athleticism, forward craft, marking ability and nose for the goals make him a constant threat in attack. The main on-field query is Butler’s running capacity, which may limit his ability to play in the midfield. A broken collarbone cut short his championships, and it is unclear when he will next play. Butler’s grandfather, Allan Davis, played in St Kilda’s 1966 flag.

Advertisement

3. Van Hattum is in the Sean Darcy mould as a hulking big man, but more athletic and skilled, which is why he is so coveted. His kicking skills are rare for a ruckman and his follow-up work is Brodie Grundy-like. That said, there is still some nervousness about using such a high selection on Van Hattum. Recruiters would love to see him mark the ball more, particularly as a down-the-line option, and don’t believe he is as athletic as Nic Naitanui, Luke Jackson or Cooper Duff-Tytler. Some scouts are glad they won’t have to make the call on Van Hattum, but the upside is enormous. 4. Gus Teixeira

Advertisement

There is so much to like about “Tex”, who is likened to Adelaide’s Josh Rachele. He lights up games with his power and creativity, and generates scoring opportunities with his penetrating kicking inside 50. Footballers who can make an impact both in attack and the midfield are prized in the AFL, and that is what Teixeira projects to be, particularly if he improves his endurance. His GPS numbers suggest he is not there yet, and explain why he doesn’t have as many prolific games as others – but he could be a match-winner in short order. 5. This is lower than Walker’s name appears on most of these lists, and the extreme likelihood is the Blues will need to match a bid at No.2. The son of Andrew – the second pick in the 2003 draft – is a good size, competitive, combative, powerful, finds the Sherrin easily and can run all day, so there are plenty of high-end traits that will ensure he is a long-term fixture in Carlton’s midfield. However, Walker’s kicking and decision-making will determine how effective and damaging he is at AFL level – and both are question marks at this stage. 6.

Advertisement

This might not be high enough. Drever has carried a titanic load and been ultra-consistent for the Rebels in the Talent League, and impressed again throughout the championships, outside Country’s disappointing performance against Metro. He is a big midfielder who impacts the game inside and outside the contest, can tuck the ball under his arm and burst away, or get it to his boot quickly, but, like Cody Walker, needs to tidy up his kicking at times, including around goal. Drever’s high-end character only adds to his value. 7. Don’t be surprised if Matthews attracts a top-five bid – he is that good. A foot injury meant Matthews appeared just twice at the championships, but he made his mark, particularly with his 35-disposal binge against Vic Country. He is a certain top-10 selection and has racked up possessions for fun all season, averaging 35 touches in the Talent League and not looking out of place in a VFL appearance, either. Matthews is a gut runner, makes quick and generally good decisions, and drives the Sherrin forward at every opportunity off his reliable left boot.

Advertisement

8. Mellody has fans inside the top five, but probably lands in the second half of the top 10 on draft night. He transformed his reputation with a blistering championships display that scored him the Larke Medal as the best-performed player. Mellody was previously pigeonholed as someone who could play on the wing or at half-back as a receiver with silky skills, but his midfield performances for WA blew that out of the water. He swung games when he went in there, and could be in the frame for West Coast’s top pick. 9. Wil Malady

Advertisement

It is all about the upside with Malady, whose “wow” moments are as exciting as anyone in this draft. His aerial prowess is eye-catching, but he isn’t a big ball-winner, so now recruiters are watching to see if the consistent impact follows in the backend of the season. Malady played as a rangy forward and on the wing for Country, but some think he could also be effective as an interceptor. He projects as a third tall in attack at AFL level. There will be some risk with picking Malady, but his potential should be too tempting for him to fall much further than this. 10. Clancy Snell Snell is the consensus best key defender in this class, although some have Mitch Harris ahead of him. His championships left questions on his lockdown defending, although he was regularly under siege in Country’s backline. Snell’s intercepting talents are undoubted, he is good enough athletically, an ideal size, and a good kick. A key defender-needy club might grab him earlier than this, but there could be at least three tall defenders selected in the first round, including Tyson Bradley, so there is depth at the position this year. 11. Caylen Murray (Brisbane Lions academy)

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘It’s been a real challenge for Bobby:’ Pies part ways with flag hero in sad circumstances Brisbane Lions Academy/Allies

Defender/midfielder, 181cm

DOB: 16/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 24 disposals, 5 rebound 50s, 5.5 contested possessions Not everyone rates Murray this highly, but he could attract a top-10 bid, which would make it difficult, or even unlikely, for the Lions to match. His stocks improved at the championships, in part thanks to his positional versatility, but also his numerous AFL traits, as he became the Allies’ sole All-Australian. Murray was a strong performer down back, where he turned defence into offence with his marking, kicking skills, dare – including one triple-bounce effort – agility and pace. He also kicked two goals against South Australia after going forward. 12. Mitch Harris Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

Key defender, 196cm

DOB: 1/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 8.8 disposals, 5 contested possessions, 1.5 intercept marks

Advertisement

Unlike last year’s draft, where Carlton’s Harry Dean was a clear standout, there are options for clubs wanting a high-end key defender. Harris is arguably the best one-on-one defender in it, and often compared to combative Gold Coast backman Sam Collins. He does not offer the same offensive value as Snell, but that doesn’t bother most scouts, given his lockdown proficiency and marking ability at a priority position. Harris might last slightly longer than this, but it is difficult to imagine him slipping outside the top 15. 13. Leo Steed Swan Districts/Western Australia

Midfielder, 177cm

DOB: 7/3/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 23.5 disposals, 10.3 contested possessions, 4.3 clearances Good luck finding someone who doesn’t like or rate Steed. He might not have the highest ceiling among the 2026 draft prospects, but is ultra-professional, a hard worker and thrives in the contest, where his toughness, fast feet and handballing come to the fore. Steed will start at half-forward in the AFL, but should eventually challenge for a midfield spot. You can’t have three players of his stature in the same midfield, but he is driven enough to find his niche. Lachie Neale has helped change opinions on sub-180-centimetre onballers. Leo Steed in action for WA at the championships. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Advertisement

14. Jake Eime Central District/South Australia

Defender, 183cm

DOB: 29/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 20.3 disposals, 4.5 rebound 50s, 3.3 intercept possessions Eime’s draft range starts about here through to the mid-20s, in what is an even section of the draft. He turned heads and changed some opinions on him, particularly with his competitiveness, with a stellar under-18 carnival down back for the South Australians. Eime wants the Sherrin in his hands (he regularly took the kick-ins), takes the game on – whether using his speed or mixing in a sidestep – and has improved his kicking, although it can be tested under pressure. He might need to reduce his risk-taking in the AFL, but that is part of his appeal. 15. Jack Pickett Jack Pickett is tackled during an AFL Futures match last year. via Getty Images

Advertisement

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Key forward, 193cm

DOB: 6/3/2008

U18 Talent League stats (averages): 5 disposals, 3 marks, 2 goals This is an aggressive ranking, and there are recruiters who have him closer to 20 because of the risk involved in drafting someone off an ACL and MCL rupture – but he was in top-five contention pre-setback. The season-ending injury happened innocuously at a Falcons training session after he kicked two goals in the first round of the Talent League. Pickett had everyone’s attention from a bottom-age year when he booted 31 goals in eight matches. He is difficult to stop, whether charging forward on a lead or standing under a high ball in a pack. 16. Sam Gayfer Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Key forward, 194cm

DOB: 21/5/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 11 disposals, 2.5 goals, 7.5 score involvements It will be interesting to see whether Pickett or Gayfer is off the board first. The nephew of Collingwood premiership defender Mick does not come with the same injury risk, which is why some scouts think he is the safer option. Gayfer enjoyed a good championships, kicking four goals against South Australia before three more – all by quarter-time – in Metro’s huge win over Country. He isn’t as athletic as others, but thrives on the physical stuff, including crashing packs and standing his ground under skied passes.

Advertisement

17. Khaled El Souki (Western Bulldogs NGA) Western Jets/Vic Metro

Forward, 176cm

DOB: 4/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 10 disposals, 5 tackles, 1 goal Khaled El Souki completes the 20m sprint test. AFL Photos via Getty Images A broken ankle sustained before the championships meant El Souki’s sole appearance was in Metro’s landslide victory over Country. He might not have been prolific, but he hit the scoreboard and made his mark with defensive pressure, including some bruising tackles. El Souki is powerful and typically a goalkicking machine, who has averaged 18 disposals and three goals in the Talent League this season. He would be a wonderful fit in the Bulldogs’ forward line, but they might not be able to match a bid if they trade for Port Adelaide star Zak Butters. 18. Noah Williams

Advertisement

Geelong Falcons/Vic Country

Midfielder/defender, 176cm

DOB: 22/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 15.5 disposals, 5.3 contested possessions, 3.3 intercept possessions Williams was once touted as a potential top-10 selection, but is no longer certain to be a first-round pick. There is a query on whether he can be a midfielder at AFL level, meaning he might need to make it as a defender or pressure forward. He is fast, aggressive, competitive, works hard, and his kicking can be very good, but is also scrappy at times. Williams’ championships performances left recruiters wanting to see more, so he needs a strong finish to the year to reassert himself. 19. Kodah Edwards South Adelaide/South Australia

Midfielder/forward, 184cm

DOB: 25/7/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 22 disposals, 3.8 clearances, 7.3 score involvements Edwards is a polarising prospect with a wide draft range that could see him drift a bit at the draft. South Australia’s captain has admirers, can play through the midfield and up forward, thrives in contested situations, and performed well in his senior debut this year for South Adelaide. But he is not as good a runner – the biggest and most common knock on him – or as athletic as other midfielders in the first-round mix. Edwards will likely start as a forward in the AFL, and still has a bit to prove on how transferable his skillset will be.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The 39 minutes that showed why the Cats have the wood over the Pies 20. Toby Krasna Northern Knights/Vic Metro

Wingman, 181cm

DOB: 28/2/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 19 disposals, 3.7 inside 50s, 1 goal Krasna was one of the biggest risers out of the championships. He may end up being taken slightly after this, but comfortably sits in the top 30. Krasna makes quick decisions when necessary, is composed under pressure, tough to tackle with his nimble footwork, and might only be slight, but is willing to wear contact. He kicks the ball well and creatively, and slotted a goal in all three of his matches at the carnival, which was another tick for him. Krasna sat out the last match with hamstring soreness. 21. Harrison Chapman

Advertisement

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

Wingman, 190cm

DOB: 6/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 18.7 disposals, 3 inside 50s, 6.7 score involvements Chapman is another with a wide draft range that starts far earlier than this, but ends significantly lower. He is a great size and beautiful mover who saved his best match of the championships for last with 18 disposals, a goal and nine score involvements in Metro’s comfortable win over Country. Chapman could end up well inside the top 20 if he produces more games like that in the months ahead, but is yet to prove he can consistently do that. Scouts would also like to see him be cleaner and more competitive in the contest and improve his ball security. 22. Tyson Bradley Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Key defender, 196cm

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 14.5 disposals, 5 rebound 50s, 3.3 intercept marks Bradley won Metro’s MVP award after a consistent campaign that put him in first-round contention and among the top group of tall defenders with Clancy Snell and Mitch Harris. He is regarded as a high IQ backman, gobbles up intercept marks and is already physically developed. However, Bradley is not quick and limited athletically, including with his lateral movement, which could leave him vulnerable against the AFL’s best forwards. His smarts help make up for that, and he is compared to Jacob Weitering and Tom Barrass for his defensive craft.

Advertisement

23. Jack Slattery Woodville-West Torrens/South Australia

Key forward, 192cm

DOB: 27/9/2007

U18 champs stats (averages): 11.3 disposals, 4.3 marks, 4 goals Slattery bolted up draft boards with an outstanding championships where his 16 goals led everyone. He was overlooked in last year’s draft and turns 19 in September, so that needs to be baked into his performance – but he could hardly have done more. Slattery showed off his set-shot proficiency with a series of brilliant finishes from all angles in a six-goal explosion against the Allies, opportunistically added five more versus Metro, then snapped two beauties from four majors at Country’s expense. Recruiters want to see him play in the Eagles’ senior side down the stretch. 24. Lochie Burrows Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Utility, 181cm

DOB: 16/9/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 13.5 disposals, 4 intercept possessions, 4 score involvements

Advertisement

There is some projection required here because Burrows’ raw numbers – even in the Talent League – don’t jump off the page, but he has many of the physical gifts and traits to be an impact player at AFL level. He leaves opponents in the dust with his acceleration, uses his pace effectively, is elusive in traffic, can play at either end or through the midfield, makes quick decisions – particularly by hand – and kicks the ball well. Burrows could end up being a weapon as a high half-forward, where his speed and marking prowess make him dangerous. 25. Ethan Herbert North Adelaide/South Australia

Ruckman, 201cm

DOB: 1/11/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 15.8 disposals, 10.8 contested possessions, 6 clearances Ethan Herbert (left) and Wil Dawson compete in an AFL national academy match. via Getty Images There are recruiters who won’t consider Herbert in this range due to doubts about his role at the highest level, but he may also go earlier. AFL coaches are increasingly turning to giants near or beyond 210 centimetres to ruck for them, so the centre bounce will be Herbert’s greatest challenge. South Australia mainly operated with Jobe Janeway as its No.1 big man, leaving Herbert to show scouts how he can fare elsewhere. His ground-ball work, clean skills and athleticism help make him an extra midfielder, while some scouts feel he could be a key defender.

Advertisement

26. George Dimer Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

Forward, 173cm

DOB: 21/6/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 16 disposals, 8.7 score involvements, 3.3 tackles Dimer’s stature won’t help his cause, but his excellent championships propelled him into top-30 contention, although some view him as a later pick. He is suited to the modern game with his combination of speed, endurance and general athleticism, while he routinely reads the play quicker than his opponents. Dimer might not be a massive goalkicker himself, but has generated so many scoring opportunities this year, whether at the championships, in the Talent League or captaining Haileybury College in school footy. The next Gryan Miers? 27. Jackson Phillips Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

Midfielder/wingman, 184cm

DOB: 30/1/2008

U18 champs stats (averages): 16.3 disposals, 3.3 inside 50s, 3.3 tackles

Advertisement

Phillips spent most of the championships on a wing, which frustrated some recruiters hoping to see how he would go in an inside role. He is a skilful player, highlighted by a slick left-handed pick-up before drilling a goal on the run from 50 metres against Western Australia, but he also missed targets at times going inside 50. title: ‘A life fully lived’: Rock journalist and cultural commentator, Glenn A. Baker, dies aged 74
text:
Advertisement

Glenn A. Baker, an Australian rock music journalist, collector, commentator, author and broadcaster, has died. He was 74. A long-time contributor to the Herald and The Age, Baker died of old age on Friday morning, his son Orson told this masthead. Glenn A. Baker among his 50,000 records in the Penrith warehouse in 2024. Louise Kennerley “Glenn had an amazing life,” Orson said. “He was so deeply involved in the music industry that we are talking about a man who absolutely had a life fully lived.” He told the ABC earlier that Baker had experienced a “period of illness” and was “declining for a while”.

Advertisement

Born in 1952, Baker grew up in Sydney and Canberra, his love for rock music sparked when at age 12 when he saw evening news coverage of The Beatles arriving at Mascot Airport for their 1964 Australian tour. “Just seeing them, hearing a burst of their music, changed my view of everything, and even though I couldn’t afford to buy the records, I could walk into a record shop and actually touch the brown Parlophone sleeves, which also carried releases by The Easybeats and The Hollies,” Baker told Peter FitzSimons in 2024. A portrait of Baker by artist Nafisa Naomi won the Packing Room Prize in the 2010 Archibald Prize. Getty Baker often credited his long career in music journalism to the first time he heard Bob Dylan’s Like A Rolling Stone a year later. He would recall this moment as an epiphany, whereupon hearing Dylan’s lyrics, Baker decided to dedicate his own life to words. He started working in the music industry in 1972 after founding the band Ol’ 55 in Sydney’s Sutherland Shire. Baker spent more than 20 years as the Australian editor of Billboard, contributed to more than 200 magazines, including Rolling Stone, authored more than 20 books and regularly featured on Australian radio, as well as writing for this masthead.

Advertisement

Orson said he remembers his father as having the “power of the pen”. “He became quite a prolific journalist and that fed from his absolute passion for music,” Orson said. “But [he] then found himself travelling so frequently to see shows or meet artists that he started to actually write travel pieces, and so the second half of his career was not just music, but he became an accomplished travel writer.” Related Article Australian music This music journalist amassed 50,000 records. Now he’s selling all of them “He wrote nonstop. In fact, I’m just going through all of his different writings right now … In his later years, he became known as the guy that when you met him, he gives you a copy of one of his books because he had so many to spare.”

Advertisement

In 2024, Baker, a fierce collector of records, CDs, books, magazines, newspaper clippings and other rock music ephemera, put his record collection up for auction – which had an estimated 80,000 items. Among with his vast collection of records, Baker had a reputation for accumulating stories about rock stars, including how he once walked right into Fleetwood Mac’s Stevie Nicks, knocking her over. Or when he met Fidel Castro at a poolside bar in Cuba with Jimmy Buffett of Margaritaville fame. Baker was also well known for always donning variously coloured fezes – Ottoman-era Turkish headwear. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Among Glenn A. Baker’s greatest hits was knocking over Stevie Nicks Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “I first wore it for fun for the cover of one of my travel books, sitting upon the engine of a 747 – they had to get a ladder to get me up there – and then when I went out to do interviews about it, people would say, ‘Oh, where’s the hat? You look great in the hat!’” Baker told Peter FitzSimons in 2024.

title: ‘Not my signature’: Anytime Fitness probes false signatures on contracts
text:
Advertisement

Exclusive BusinessCompaniesConsumer rights ‘Not my signature’: Anytime Fitness probes false signatures on contracts Elias Visontay July 31, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anytime Fitness has apologised over a string of incidents in which customers were signed up to branches with false signatures inserted into contracts they’d never seen, while others were made to sign blank agreements before terms of their memberships were added. New customers attempting to join Anytime Fitness centres in NSW and Queensland have lodged separate complaints this week about contracting practices at the gym franchise, which has more than 780,000 members across more than 600 premises in Australia. Michael Fraser’s fake signature. Anytime Fitness is investigating after customers’ signatures were falsified and inserted into contracts the clients had never seen. Matt Willis Michael Fraser had been growing dissatisfied with his longtime gym on the Gold Coast when, in mid-June, he inquired with a soon-to-launch Anytime Fitness in the suburb of Biggera Waters, a more convenient location for him. He was offered a discounted rate over the phone and broadly agreed to the offer. Fraser was asked to leave his payment details with the club to reserve the terms as an inaugural member of the gym.

Advertisement

He was told that when the branch finally opened, he could go into the gym, show his ID, complete an orientation and pre-exercise questionnaire, before reading and signing a contract outlining his membership terms. But on Tuesday, an email landed in his inbox claiming his membership had started, and his signed contract was attached, despite Fraser having had no further direct dealings with the gym. The false signature, which mimicked handwriting, appeared three times throughout the contract, which included terms he felt were not reflected in the initial phone call he’d had with the gym. It resembled the template signatures available in common contract-management software. “I just knew it wasn’t my signature, I don’t put dots between my initials,” Fraser said. His colleague, Maddison Johnstone, who had also given her details, keen to sign up when the gym opened, similarly received an email about 24 hours later with a contract containing signatures that were not hers.

Advertisement

“I have never been sent an unsigned copy, and have never read or even sighted it. I never provided my signature, digital or otherwise,” said Johnstone, who was also surprised the length of the contract was 18 months. “It is something I would never have signed.” Related Article Consumer rights Gyms push back on law change that would ease cancellation “The gym isn’t open yet, so I am not sure how four weeks free starting yesterday makes sense,” Johnstone said. Fraser and Johnstone are co-founders of Operation Redress, a consumer advocacy firm which has raised whistleblower concerns to push for reforms of systemic issues of laws governing franchise businesses. Fraser’s advocacy has included raising concerns surrounding what became a major wage fraud scandal for 7/11. After Fraser aired a complaint about his experiences, Anytime Fitness launched an investigation. Its Australian chief executive, Simon Thompson, called Fraser directly on Wednesday.

Advertisement

An Anytime Fitness spokeswoman confirmed it had begun an internal investigation into the contracts. “Given the serious nature of this matter, we are reviewing all relevant documentation, systems, and processes to establish the facts,” they said. Fraser and Johnstone’s experience is similar but separate to what Rachel Sarfatij alleges happened to her when signing up for the Anytime Fitness branch in the Sydney suburb of Randwick. She had been going to a Fitness First but in an inconvenient location, and was wooed by a $6-per-week-for-six-weeks deal at Anytime. “I went in, talked to them, got the spiel, agreed on a price and a year time frame.” Sarfatij mentioned that she lived close to another Anytime location, and may visit that branch more, something the employee said would not be an issue.

Advertisement

She was then handed an iPad and asked to sign on a screen in which only the signature box, and not the rest of the contract, was visible.“I couldn’t see anything that I was signing, but I figured we had just verbally agreed on the terms, what else were they going to do?” Immediately after signing, Sarfatij claims the employee then told her that if she went to another branch more frequently than the Randwick one, her membership would automatically shift there and she’d have to pay different fees. She was also made to pay $69.95 for an electronic key fob to enter the gym. When Sarfatij received the full contract via email, all the boxes that normally outline the details of a membership were unpopulated. Outside of her signature, the contract was essentially blank. After a back and forth, Sarfatij said the gym manager admitted there was a technical issue, and Sarfatij asked to cancel her contract, which was within a seven-day cooling-off period.

Advertisement

“I had such a bad feeling in my stomach, I don’t trust being stuck in a contract with this gym,” she said. Related Article Home loans Home owners warned to check offset accounts after $55 million interest issue But the manager emailed Sarfatij to refuse to return the almost $70 she had paid for the key. “As outlined in the membership agreement you signed, the key fob fee is non-refundable,” the manager wrote. Citing a term in a contract the gym admitted Sarfatij never saw infuriated her. “If they admit the mistake with the contract, how can they refuse me a refund?” The Anytime spokeswoman said there had been an intermittent technical issue with the third-party software it uses to populate membership agreements.

Advertisement

“While the technical issue has been resolved, it does not excuse the way the situation was handled … we regret the inconvenience caused,” the spokeswoman said. Sarfatij is yet to a receive a refund. Speaking more broadly on the contract claims, the spokeswoman said: “We certainly take any matter relating to the integrity of our membership processes and the member experience extremely seriously. “It’s disappointing that a situation like this can impact the trust our members, franchisees and club teams have worked hard to build over the past 18 years. That’s why we’ll take every necessary step to investigate thoroughly, establish the facts, and take action where appropriate,” the spokeswoman said. title: ‘Are you serious?’: Claim in ICAC probe
text:
The co-founder of a secretive religious movement working to bolster its ranks within the NSW Liberal Party "always seemed to have a way around things", another member has told an explosive anti-corruption inquiry that has so far named leading figures including Angus Taylor.

The eight-week probe at the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption is examining whether the brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet, Jean-Claude Perrottet, as well as Liberal powerbrokers Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Robert Assaf, solicited or accepted political donations, including from prohibited donors, for the recruitment and/or renewal of Liberal Party members.

The four men were involved in what was self-described as "the Reformers", a group within the NSW Liberal Party right that sought to expand the number of conservative and Christian members in regional and metropolitan branches.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Federal Opposition Leader Mr Taylor is not a party in the investigation and has denied providing funds to the group. Neither Mr Taylor or Dominic Perrottet are accused of any wrongdoing.

Robert Assaf, a co-founder of the group, returned to the witness box on Friday and was grilled over the Reformers' handling of donations, including from prominent hotelier Michael O'Hara, who bankrolled the group until a falling out over Covid mandates.

Robert Assaf co-founded the Reformers with Christian Ellis. Picture: NewWire / Rohan Kelly

'Tricky way to do things'

The commission was told a Westpac account was initially set up in the name of the Reformers.

However, after Mr Ellis' lobbying firm Beckington, which also did work with Catholic Schools NSW – which provided Beckington with a monthly retainer, the commission was told – was set up, it was "funnelled through there instead".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Assaf told counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC that he could "recall some discussions about the best way to keep the donations from Mr O'Hara going to the maximum benefit from a tax perspective".

"We're not a registered charity, so it's not tax deductible to donate to the Reformers' bank account, so there must have been some idea that Christian had at the time (that) this is a better way to do it," Mr Assaf said.

Asked about a conversation with Mr Ellis about creating "fake invoices so that Mr O'Hara could get a tax deduction", Mr Assaf said it was "an example".

Pressed for any more, Mr Assaf said "you'd have to ask" someone else.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The answer prompted a rebuke from Ms Dwyer, who said "Mr Assaf, you have a degree from a university, don't you … and you have filled out tax returns yourself?"

Lawyer and hotelier Michael O'Hara once bankrolled the group. Picture: NewsWire / Damian Shaw

"Are you seriously suggesting that in 2020 you did not know that you had to declare tax deductions in accordance with the law?"

Mr Assaf replied: "Well, if you don't really understand the law, you don't think you're breaking it.

"But in the sense of tax, I would have thought it was a way to minimise tax at the time, which now I know it is not."

Asked if he thought creating fake invoices was legal, Mr Assaf said, "No, it's not right."

"In 2020, did you think it might be right?" Ms Dwyer asked.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I think I thought I just want to trust that whoever said to me at the time, 'I know everyone does a little, it's OK. It's a tricky way to do things'," Mr Assaf replied.

Asked if Mr Ellis had told him in October 2020 that it was a "tricky way to do things", Mr Assaf said, "No, not about the specific scenario, but he (Mr Ellis) always seemed to have a way around things."

Payments 'disguised'

The commission was told Mr O'Hara had not ever asked for the payments to Beckington to be disguised.

However, in October 2020, Mr Ellis "took over" and he "gave receipt to Mr O'Hara suggesting that he was doing some consultancy work for him, which was false".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Assaf denied the intention was to "conceal" the payments.

"Well, it definitely wasn't good accounting," he said.

"I don't think anyone was thinking like that … no one was (thinking) they were doing anything wrong."

Mr Assaf said he accepted "from a tax perspective … now that I know more", it was not right.

However, when pressed by Assistant Commissioner Fabian Gleeson whether it was right from an "honesty perspective", Mr Assaf said it was "tricky".

Earlier, Mr Assaf, who worked for various federal parliamentarians, including Tony Abbott, admitted he was "aware" of electoral laws covering political donations.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC grilled Mr Assaf. Picture: NewsWire / Damian Shaw

"I would have attended at least one fundraiser I can recall where a (declaration) form like that was filled in, although I don't know if they were always filled in because if they were below a certain amount, maybe you didn't need to. I can't recall," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Later, Mr Assaf continued: "I was never introduced to the electoral laws in detail because I was always seen as an internal machination Liberal Party person.

"There were always other people who dealt with that when it came money coming into the party.

"I'll tell you what, if someone told me any point before I got my first summons to this, that what I had done was a problem, I would have gone straight to the Electoral Commission and recorded it and sorted it out."

Mr Assaf denied Mr Ellis telling him it was "no problem", stating "we've never had those discussions".

The commission was told payments were made by Beckington to Mr Assaf's wife, Carmel Assaf, who there were discussions about being made director of Beckington in August 2019.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Asked why Ms Assaf would need to be director to receive a "referral fee" – something Mr Assaf said he also received – Mr Assaf said "it would be some tricky thing about the organisation".

Reformers probed

By 2021, the Reformers had recruited an additional 1000 members to the Liberal Party, the commission was told.

Mr Assaf agreed those efforts benefited the Liberal Party "first by improving its financial position because money went into their coffers".

"That's one observation that could be made, I suppose, from recruitment activity," Mr Assaf said.

Ms Dwyer continued: "And it also increased the number of Liberal Party members who would likely participate in party activities like campaigning and fundraising in the future."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"That's another observation. That's correct," Mr Assaf replied.

Dylan Whitelaw, a former associate of the Reformers and employee of Catholic Schools NSW, and Mr O'Hara have previously given evidence before the commission.

Mr Whitelaw outlined the group's alleged activities, including the work undertaken by himself and Mr Assaf for the Reformers while employed by Catholic Schools NSW.

The hearing was also told Mr Whitelaw on March 11, 2021 sent a message in which he told the group chat that "Dallas has told me he got commitment from Angus for the $15k injection plus a $3k monthly donation!"

Dylan Whitelaw, a former associate of the Reformers and employee of Catholic Schools NSW. Picture: NewsWire/ Gaye Gerard

Asked about the claims on Friday, Mr Taylor said: "As I've said, I am not going to provide a running commentary."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The probe is also examining the relationship between fugitive property developer Jean Nassif – including donations allegedly made to "damage to the political career of" Liberal MP David Elliott and remoe of Building Commissioner David Chandler – and Catholic Schools NSW former chief executive Dallas McInerney, who has since stood aside.

It will also examine whether Labor Strathfield councillors Sharangan Maheswaran – an employee of Mr Nassif – and Karen Pensabene engaged in breaches of public trust, including potential blackmail and breaches of surveillance device laws.

Mr Maheswaran is alleged to have potentially participated in attempts to "discredit" Mr Chandler and adopted "a similar tactic" to thwart a political rival – independent councillor Matthew Blackmore – by attempting to build a "dirt file and threatening a professional attack if he did not bend to his wishes, including by use of material gathered by the same private investigator he had hired to assist Mr Nassif".

ICAC does not make findings of criminal conduct. Instead, following the hearing, individuals may be referred to the NSW Director of Public Prosecutions.

title: Aussie frontline worker 'angry and helpless' as he battles homelessness crisis: 'Worst in 50 years'
text:
It's no surprise to one worker on the front lines that most Aussies have homelessness on their mind, as he helps to battle a crisis that is the worst he has ever seen.

"I have been working with homeless people for over 50 years, and I have never seen it as serious as now," Reverend Bill Crews told Yahoo News.

The Rev. Bill Crews Foundation CEO said he feels "angry and helpless" as he sees more Australians experiencing or coming close to being unhoused.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Recent stats show nearly 90 per cent of people in the country see homelessness as a serious issue, while just over 54 per cent worry that they or someone close to them could face homelessness or housing insecurity in the next few years, according to Primara Research.

It said the concern is led by Gen X (60 per cent), then Gen Z (58 per cent) and Millennials (55 per cent), dropping sharply among Boomers (43 per cent).

Those living in Queensland (59 per cent) and NSW (59 per cent) are considered the "most anxious states".

Confronting stats on homelessness in Australia

But, you don't need statistics to prove how concerning the homelessness crisis is to Australia, Bill said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It's visual to everybody.

"Just the sheer numbers of people sleeping on the streets, it's obvious to so many people that there are more people than ever sleeping on the streets."

As Bill walks through his restaurant in Sydney, serving meals to disadvantaged Aussies, or passes by the lines outside, he said he's heard from a number of people who've said, "I never expected to be here, and here I am".

The CEO of the Reverend Bill Crews Foundation says the homelessness crisis in Australia is severe and says he has noticed significantly more people sleeping on the streets, including women and families. Source: Rev. Bill Crews Foundation

About 46 per cent of Australians have said they've noticed more homelessness locally in the past year. Primara Research found in states like Queensland and Western Australia, it was most noticeable.

What is increasingly worrisome is seeing those who are donating supplies and those who are in need of supplies, both "just as anxious about being homeless", Bill said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The reason [some people are] eating in the restaurant is because they're trying to hold the homes they got."

At certain times of the year, the foundation has seen 39 per cent more people in need of a free meal here than they did a year ago, Bill added.

Why are Aussies worried about homelessness today?

Bill said he regularly hears from Aussies who are making tough decisions, such as whether to pay for food or medical bills.

Research has shown most people (84 per cent) blame rising rents and the cost of living as a main reason homelessness is becoming more visible and confronting for Aussies.

Bill is emphasising the importance of building more houses across the country and is critical of the government's response. Source: Rev. Bill Crews Foundation

Structural changes are a must to resolve "decades-long problems," Bill said, as the impact of rising living costs is weighing heavily on Australians.

'Government lacks urgency in addressing housing crisis'

He emphasises the importance of building more houses, but remains critical of state and federal governments, suggesting they lack urgency.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

It's why he has been calling for a ministry or ombudsman for homelessness, "because without that direct attachment to government, nothing happens".

Unless governments act, Bill said, five years from now, he expects homelessness in the country "will be at least as bad as it is now".

RELATED:

Primara Research reported that Australians believed the top priorities for governments in responding to homelessness should be rent controls (21.4 per cent), building more social and public housing (19.1), and faster construction methods.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The public looks to government, Canberra above all, and although they name domestic violence and mental health as the main drivers of who becomes homeless, their demanded solutions centre firmly on housing and rent," Primara said.
